Synergy, Diversity & Sustainability reflects Coal India’s approach to 
creating enduring value by bringing together the scale and capabilities of its subsidiaries, people, infrastructure and strategic partnerships. Despite moderated production and full-year profitability, the Company’s stronger fourth-quarter performance demonstrated the resilience of its core 
operations and its ability to navigate evolving demand conditions.
This theme signals a broader pathway to long-term growth and value creation. Coal India is progressively expanding into 
renewable energy, power generation, coal gasification, fertilisers and critical minerals, while advancing responsible mining 
and resource efficiency. Together, these priorities aim to diversify future revenue streams, strengthen business resilience and 
position the Company for India’s evolving energy landscape

Coal India at a Glance 
Coal India Limited (CIL) is a Maharatna Central Public Sector Enterprise 
and the world’s largest coal-producing company. Through our mining operations spread across the country's major coal-bearing regions, we play a critical role in supporting India's energy requirements by supplying coal to the power, steel, cement and other industrial sectors.
To emerge as a global player in the primary 
energy sector committed to provide 
energy security to the country by attaining 
environmentally & socially sustainable growth 
through best practices from mine to market.To produce and market the planned 
quantity of coal and coal products efficiently 
and economically in an ecofriendly manner with due regard to safety, 
conservation and quality.
Scale and Market 
Presence

portfolio of Mining assets.Integrated Mining

=== page 12 ===
India’s energy landscape is undergoing a structural transition driven by rising electricity demand,  
energy security priorities and reduced dependence on imported fuels. While the energy mix is gradually diversifying,coal 
remains central to ensuring reliable baseload power for industrial and economic growth.
During FY 2025-26, thermal power plants increasingly substituted imported coal with domestic coal through higher 
blending, reflecting stronger policy focus on self-reliance, cost optimisation and supply security. This shift is creating 
new demand opportunities for domestic producers while strengthening resilience to global commodity price volatility.
5.7 GW 
Imported-coal capacity already operating on domestic coal4.3 GW
Additional capacity under trial
16 MT
Domestic coal booked by imported-coal-based generatorsStructural Shift in India’s Thermal Coal Market
India’s thermal coal market is witnessing a clear realignment in favour of domestic coal.
• Domestic coal constituted ~30% of imported coal 
based plants capacity
• Thermal coal imports declined by 12% in April 2026 viz-a-viz April 2025
Outlook
India’s energy future is expected to be shaped by a balanced mix of renewables, conventional thermal power and emerging low carbon 
technologies. Coal will continue to play a critical role in powering economic growth, ensuring energy security and supporting industrial development during this transition. As the country moves toward greater self-reliance, domestic coal producers are expected to remain central to India’s evolving energy architecture, creating long-term growth opportunities for Coal India.Policy Support for Domestic Production
Accelerated environmental clearances, mine expansion approvals and supportive policy interventions continue to improve 
production visibility and strengthen long-term 
sector fundamentals.Rising Power Demand
Rapid urbanisation, industrial expansion, 
digital infrastructure growth and rising 
household consumption continue to drive 
electricity demand upward. Reliable thermal 
generation remains essential to maintain 
grid stability and meet peak demand.
Energy Security Imperative
Geopolitical volatility and fluctuating 
international coal prices have reinforced 
the importance of domestic fuel security. 
Policymakers are increasingly focused on reducing import dependence and 
strengthening indigenous resource utilisation.Infrastructure Expansion
Investments in railway connectivity, First Mile 
Connectivity projects, silos, mechanised 
evacuation systems and logistics infrastructure 
are improving coal evacuation efficiency and 
reducing supply bottlenecks
Market Drivers 
Shaping the 
Operating 
LandscapeOperating Environment
Strategic Implications for Coal India
The evolving operating environment presents significant opportunities 
for Coal India. Rising domestic demand from imported-coal-based 
power plants expands addressable market potential while strengthening 
long-term offtake visibility. At the same time, higher expectations around 
supply reliability, coal quality consistency and evacuation efficiency are 
reshaping competitive priorities.

Chairman’s Message 
Every achievement 
of Coal India begins with its people.  
The scale and complexity  of our operations  demand continuous capability building of our people across technical, managerial and leadership roles.
B. Sairam
Chairman -cum- Managing Director
Dear Stakeholders,
The world continues to live through a 
period of energy transition, geopolitical 
uncertainty and shifting economic 
priorities. For a country like India, the 
challenge is not only to grow, but to grow with reliability, affordability and 
resilience. Energy sits at the centre of this 
challenge. It powers homes, industries, 
transport networks, public services and 
the aspirations of a billion people.
Coal India has always understood this 
responsibility in its fullest sense. We are 
the world’s largest coal producer, but 
more importantly, we are an institution 
built around India’s energy needs. Our 
work supports electricity generation, 
industrial activity, employment, regional 
development and the wider economy. This 
role places on us a responsibility that is both operational and national.
FY 2025-26 was a year of steady performance in a demanding 
environment. Weather-related disruptions, 
evacuation constraints and local operating 
challenges affected production and 
dispatch in parts of the year. Even so, 
your Company stayed focused on supply 
assurance, mine productivity, customer 
service, financial discipline and long-term 
capacity building.
Powering India’s energy 
security
Coal continues to remain central to 
India’s energy mix. As power demand 
grows with industrialisation, urbanisation 
and rising household consumption, the 
need for reliable domestic fuel remains strong. Coal India continues to carry this responsibility with focus and scale.
During FY 2025-26, your Company 
produced 768.19 Million Tonnes of coal 
and recorded coal offtake of 744.83 Million Tonnes. Supply to the power 
sector remained our foremost priority, 
with 588.63 Million Tonnes dispatched to 
this critical segment during the year. These 
numbers underline the scale of the task we 
perform each day and the importance of 
a dependable domestic coal ecosystem.
Dispatch performance during the year 
was affected by incessant rainfall in the second quarter, railway evacuation 
constraints, rake availability issues etc. The 
response to the operational headwinds 
was marked by closer coordination across 
subsidiaries, continued engagement 
with consumers, and focused action on evacuation bottlenecks.
The e-auction platform continued to serve 
a wider base of consumers. During the 
year, 101.72 Million Tonnes were allocated 
under e-auction, compared with 89.38 
Million Tonnes in the previous year. Long-
term demand creation also continued 
through SHAKTI and the revised SHAKTI 
framework, with operative linkage 
of about 643.4 MTPA with the power 
sector and 119.2 MTPA with non-power consumers as on 31
st March 2026.
Strengthening the operating 
backbone
Long-term growth depends as much on 
infrastructure as it does on production. 
During the year, your Company 
completed three coal mining projects and 
approved 13 new coal mining projects 
with a combined capacity of nearly 77 
MTY. These investments strengthen our 
production pipeline as we progress 
towards our long-term capacity goals.
The Company is also prioritising 
expanding rail connectivity and First Mile 
Connectivity infrastructure. Nine FMC 
projects became operational during 
the year, supporting mechanised coal 
evacuation, improved logistics and 
lower environmental impact. Strategic 
partnerships with IRCON International 
Limited, Indian Port Rail & Ropeway Corporation Limited and Konkan 
Railway Corporation Limited will further 
strengthen evacuation capabilities across 
our mining operations.Delivering financial strength
Even in a year of operational challenges, 
your Company maintained strong financial 
outcomes. Coal India recorded revenue 
from operations of H 1,68,400 Crores, 
Profit Before Tax of H 41,923 Crores and 
Profit After Tax of H 31,071 Crores during 
FY 2025-26 . Net worth increased to  
H 1,19,102 Crores, while capital employed 
stood at H 2,18,009 Crores.
Your Company also continued its strong 
record of shareholder returns. During 
FY 2025-26, Coal India paid H 10,272 
Crores as dividend to Government of India 
and maintained total dividend at H 26.50 
per share, equal to 265% of face value. 
Since listing in 2010, the Company has 
distributed H 1.88 trillion to shareholders. 
Our contribution to the exchequer 
remained substantial. During the year, 
CIL and its subsidiaries paid H 52,299 
Crores towards royalty, cess, DMF, NMET, 
GST and other levies. This contribution is 
a reminder that Coal India’s value extends 
across the economy.
Unlocking enterprise value
FY 2025-26 also marked an important 
milestone in Coal India’s value unlocking 
journey. Bharat Coking Coal Limited 
was successfully listed during the year, 
receiving an overwhelming response from 
investors with an overall subscription of nearly 147 times. 
The successful listing represents 
another step towards creating focused, 
independent businesses while enhancing transparency, governance 
and market participation.
The listing of CMPDIL during the year 
further strengthened this journey. In 
addition, the Board accorded in-principle 
approval for initiating the process for 
public listing of Mahanadi Coalfields 
Limited and South Eastern Coalfields Long-term growth depends as much on 
infrastructure as it does on production. 
During the year, your Company completed 
three coal mining projects and approved 13 
new coal mining projects with a combined 
capacity of nearly 77 MTY20 21

Limited. These initiatives are expected 
to unlock long-term value while enabling 
each business to pursue its own growth 
trajectory with greater operational focus.
Investing in tomorrow’s growth
Coal India has always planned beyond 
the immediate production cycle, investing 
today to strengthen the nation’s future 
energy security. During FY2025-26, we 
continued to expand our project pipeline, 
strengthen evacuation infrastructure 
and build capabilities that will support 
sustained growth over the coming decade.
Coal gasification remained a strategic 
priority, with Talcher Fertilisers Limited, 
Bharat Coal Gasification and Chemicals 
Limited and Coal Gas India Limited 
advancing projects to convert coal into 
value-added products such as fertilisers, 
ammonium nitrate and synthetic natural 
gas. Looking ahead, we are preparing 
a broader coal gasification programme 
with significant investments to drive value 
addition and support import substitution.
The Company also accelerated its 
entry into critical minerals through the 
ongoing incorporation of overseas 
holding companies in Singapore and  
Chile, strategic partnerships with 
domestic mining organisations, and the 
allocation of a Rare Earth Elements block 
in Maharashtra. Together, these initiatives 
broaden our resource portfolio while 
supporting India’s long-term industrial 
and strategic priorities.
Advancing Research and 
Innovation
Coal India’s R&D agenda gathered 
momentum with the establishment of 
the National Centre for Coal and Energy 
Research (NaCCER), a hub-and-spoke 
modelled research centre that has 
shifted the Company’s focus from proof-
of-concept studies to TRL-4 and above 
prototype development with scalable 
industrial applications. To institutionalise 
innovation, CIL also formulated a 
comprehensive R&D Policy.
Strengthening industry-academia 
collaboration, CIL established three 
Centres of Excellence at IIT Hyderabad 
(CLEANZ), IIT Madras (CSE) and IIT (ISM) Dhanbad (IMiN). Currently, 18 
R&D projects with an outlay of about 
H 225 Crores are being executed 
under NaCCER’s oversight, alongside 
international collaborations with Ergo 
Exergy (Canada), Ericsson (Sweden), CSIRO (Australia) and the University of Wollongong (Australia). In addition, 
13 high-TRL projects involving 
pilot-scale research and prototype development, along with 11 low-TRL projects, are underway across the 
Centres of Excellence.
Expanding beyond coal
Coal will continue to anchor India’s energy 
security for years to come. At the same 
time, Coal India is creating new growth 
platforms that build on its engineering 
strengths and resource base.
Looking ahead, the Company is preparing 
a broader coal gasification programme 
with planned investments of around  
H 50,000 Crores, creating new avenues for 
value addition and import substitution.
Building the clean energy 
portfolio
Coal India continues to expand its 
presence across renewable energy and 
emerging clean energy businesses while 
maintaining its core responsibility of 
supporting India’s energy security.
During FY 2025-26, the Company 
commissioned a 100 MW solar power 
plant in Gujarat and advanced large-
scale solar projects in Rajasthan and Uttar 
Pradesh. It also secured Battery Energy 
Storage System projects in Odisha and 
Telangana, strengthening its presence 
in next-generation power infrastructure.
Alongside these initiatives, Coal India and 
Damodar Valley Corporation incorporated 
a joint venture to develop a 1,600 MW thermal power project at Chandrapura, 
reflecting the Company’s balanced approach towards conventional and 
emerging energy opportunities.
Caring for the environment
Coal India has always 
recognised that responsible  
mining extends far beyond production. 
Every operation exists within an  
ecological and social landscape, making 
environmental stewardship integral to  
the way we plan, operate and 
restore our mining assets.  
 
During FY2025-26, afforestation  
remained a key priority, with H 52.92 lakh saplings planted 
across nearly 2,404 hectares  
covering both mine lease and non mine 
areas. Miyawaki plantations were  
expanded across 51.8 hectares, creating  dense green cover in selected locations.  
Under the Government of India’s Green 
Credit Programme, more than 1,793  
hectares of degraded forest land were  
registered for plantation, extending  
ecological restoration beyond  
our operational footprint.  
 
Our water management  
initiatives also demonstrate  
how mining infrastructure can generate 
lasting value for neighbouring  
communities. Together, these efforts are 
steadily restoring mined landscapes,  
strengthening ecological resilience and 
creating sustainable community assets  
for the long term.
Safety remains our first priority
 
Mining is an inherently complex business 
where safety remains our foremost 
priority. During FY2025-26, all producing 
mines underwent comprehensive safety 
audits supported by Principal Hazard 
Management Plans, mine-specific Safety 
Management Plans, regular inspections 
and corrective actions. Safety campaigns, 
toolbox talks, pre-shift interactions and competency assessments further reinforced a strong safety culture 
across our operations.
Technology continues to strengthen our 
safety framework. Integrated Command 
and Control Centres are now operational 
across all producing subsidiaries and NEC, 
supported by AI-enabled video analytics, 
CCTV surveillance, GPS-based vehicle 
tracking, RFID-enabled access systems 
and traffic management solutions for 
real-time monitoring and faster response.
The launch of the Safety AI Analytics Dashboard further strengthened our 
ability to anticipate, monitor and manage 
operational risks through predictive 
insights. Together, these initiatives are 
enabling safer, smarter and more resilient 
mining operations across Coal India.
Investing in our people
Coal India’s achievements are built on 
the strength of its people. Supporting the 
scale and complexity of our operations 
requires continuous capability building 
across technical, managerial and leadership roles. During FY2025-26, 
over 1.02 lakh employees participated in 
training programmes, accounting for more 
than 6.09 lakh training man-days. Training 
also extended to over 46,000 contract workers, strengthening capabilities across 
the broader workforce.
Leadership development remained a key 
focus through programmes conducted 
by IIM Mumbai, IIM Lucknow, IIT Bombay 
and IIT (ISM) Dhanbad, complemented 
by international learning initiatives, 
specialised technical programmes and 
structured succession planning.
Coal India was recognised as a ‘Great 
Place to Work’ and featured among 
India’s Best Workplaces in Manufacturing, 
reflecting its continued emphasis on 
employee development, workplace 
culture and organisational excellence. 
Recruitment also remained aligned with future business needs through 
the induction of Management Trainees, 
medical professionals and specialists, 
alongside lateral hiring to strengthen renewable energy and emerging 
business capabilities.
Creating value beyond mining
Coal India has always believed that 
the communities around its operations 
should participate in the Company’s 
progress. Our CSR initiatives continue 
to focus on areas that create lasting 
impact, including healthcare, education, 
drinking water, sanitation, livelihood generation, skill development and 
community infrastructure.
During FY 2025-26, your Company spent H 1,016 Crores on Corporate 
Social Responsibility initiatives across 
the country. Programmes implemented 
through Coal India and its subsidiaries 
reached thousands of beneficiaries across 
coal-bearing districts, strengthening 
access to healthcare, quality education 
and basic infrastructure.
Healthcare remained one of the largest 
areas of intervention. The Company 
continued to support specialised healthcare programmes, hospitals, 
mobile medical services and preventive healthcare initiatives. The Nanha Sa Dil 
programme, which provides life-saving 
treatment for children with congenital 
heart disease, continued to transform 
young lives during the year and received 
the Healthcare Initiative of the Year awar d.
Strategic Future Outlook
India’s development journey will continue 
to require dependable and affordable 
energy. Coal will remain an important part of that journey, even as the country’s 
energy mix becomes more diverse.
Coal India enters this next phase from a 
position of strength. We have a strong 
resource base, an expanding project 
pipeline, healthy financials and a clear 
strategy for future growth. Alongside 
strengthening our core business, we are 
creating new opportunities across coal 
gasification, critical minerals, renewable 
energy, battery storage and power 
generation. These initiatives are gradually 
broadening the Company’s growth 
platform while remaining aligned with 
national priorities.
The road ahead will demand greater 
efficiency, faster execution and continued investment in technology, people and infrastructure. It will also 
require us to balance energy security 
with environmental responsibility and 
community development. 
These priorities are not competing objectives. Together, they define the 
future of responsible mining. As we move 
towards our long-term production target 
of around one billion Tonnes, our focus will 
remain on building an organisation that 
is operationally stronger, technologically 
more capable and better prepared for 
the changing energy landscape. Every 
investment we make today is guided  
by this objective.
Corporate Governance
As C oal India expands in scale and 
diversifies its portfolio, strong governance 
remains central to our business. The Board continued to provide strategic 
oversight across business performance, capital allocation, project execution, risk management and long-term planning.
Your Company has complied with the 
Corporate Governance Guidelines for Central Public Sector Enterprises issued by the Department of Public 
Enterprises, the applicable provisions 
of the Companies Act, 2013, and the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015, except 
for the appointment of the requisite number of Independent Directors, which rests with the Government of 
India. The matter has been taken up with 
the Ministry of Coal.
The Annual Report includes a separate 
Corporate Governance section, the 
requisite compliance certificate from a peer-reviewed Practising Company Secretary and the Secretarial Audit 
Report for FY2025-26. Guided by the 
principles of integrity, transparency and 
accountability, we continue to strengthen 
our governance framework in line with 
evolving regulatory expectations while 
creating long-term stakeholder value.
Stakeholder Appreciation
On behalf of the Board, I extend my 
sincere gratitude to the Ministry of Coal, 
Government of India, State Governments, 
our customers, Shareholders, lending 
institutions, business partners, local 
communities and every member of the 
Coal India family for their continued trust, 
support and commitment.
Our people remain the driving 
force behind every achievement. Their dedication, resilience and unwavering commitment have 
enabled Coal India to fulfil its national 
responsibility year after year.
During the West Asia crisis the stake holders continued to supply critical items like Explosives & Explosive Accessories and High Speed Diesel 
for uninterrupted production.  
Coal India has powered India’s growth 
for decades. We remain committed to 
doing so with the same sense of purpose 
while preparing the Company for the 
opportunities of tomorrow.

are broadening our role beyond coal to build new engines of growth across 
renewable energy, thermal power, energy storage and coal gasification.
While we remain committed to meeting the country’s growing energy demand through domestic coal production, we are 
simultaneously investing in future businesses that align with India’s long term energy transition and net zero ambition.
Our diversification strategy is centred on creating a balanced energy portfolio that strengthens resilience and unlocks new value pools.

stakeholders across the value chain. These include shareholders, customers, employees, regulators, government bodies, suppliers, contractors, local 
communities, civil society, media and knowledge institutions.
Our ability to create long term value depends on understanding stakeholder expectations and responding in a timely, 
transparent and responsible manner. Stakeholder engagement therefore remains integral to how we operate, manage 
risks and shape strategic priorities.

Governance Our Leadership Team
Strong governance remains fundamental to create sustainable long-term value. 
In a highly regulated sector such as mining and energy, robust governance systems enable effective decision-making, strengthen accountability and 
support responsible business conduct.
At Coal India, our governance framework supports transparent leadership, disciplined oversight and risk-aware decision-
making across all levels of the organisation. The framework is designed to align strategic priorities with regulatory 
requirements while strengthening stakeholder confidence.
Board Oversight and 
Composition

and oversight across business operations, 
capital allocation, risk management and 
long-term value creation. Its diverse 
composition brings together sector expertise, governance experience and independent oversight, enabling 
balanced and informed decision-making.

focused supervision across critical areas 
including audit, stakeholder relationships, 
nomination and remuneration, CSR, 
and risk oversight.Board Committees

Disciplinary or Punitive Actions TakenEthical Conduct and Vigilance 
Our vigilance function upholds 
compliance, accountability and integrity 
across all levels of the organisation. 
The central Vigilance Division, led by 
the Chief Vigilance Officer (CVO) at our 
Kolkata headquarters, works closely with 
subsidiary-level CVOs and the Ministry of 
Coal to ensure effective oversight.
Investigations are conducted in 
accordance with the Conduct, Discipline 
and Appeal (CDA) Rules, with cases escalated to the appropriate criminal 
enforcement agencies where required. 
Beyond enforcement, we place strong 
emphasis on awareness, capacity building and training initiatives to 
promote a culture of ethics and integrity 
across the organisation and among 
external stakeholders.Internal Controls and 
Assurance 
A robust internal control environment 
supports financial discipline, operational 
reliability and regulatory compliance. 
Periodic audits, assurance reviews 
and control assessments help identify 
improvement areas and strengthen 
governance effectiveness.
Together, these systems enhance resilience and support disciplined 
execution across the enterprise.
Whistle blower Protection
Our Whistleblower Policy enables employees, vendors and other stakeholders to report concerns confidentially and without fear of 
retaliation. The policy accepts both named 
and anonymous disclosures, ensures 
impartial investigation of all concerns, 
and reinforces our commitment to 
transparency and ethical conduct
Stakeholder Engagement and 
Ethical Practices.
We actively engage with stakeholders 
through public meetings, helplines and 
digital platforms, ensuring our governance 
framework reflects community 
perspectives, customer feedback and 795
Complaints Resolved supplier accountability. Anti-corruption 
clauses are embedded in vendor contracts, while CVC-recommended Integrity Pacts are implemented for high-value procurements, extending our commitment to ethical conduct 
across the value chain.
Risk Management 
Coal India operates in a dynamic 
environment shaped by regulatory 
developments, operational complexities, 
market shifts, technological change and 
evolving sustainability expectations. 
Effective risk management is therefore 
essential to protecting enterprise value and enabling resilient growth.
Our Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework enables systematic 
identification, assessment, prioritisation 
and mitigation of risks across operations, 
projects and strategic initiatives.
Risk Management Approach 
Risk management is embedded into strategic planning and operational 
decision-making through a structured 
and continuous process.
 Risk Identification 
Emerging and existing risks are identified across business functions, subsidiaries and operating environments.
 Risk Assessment 
Risks are assessed based on likelihood, potential impact and business criticality.
 Risk Prioritisation 
Material risks are prioritised based on enterprise exposure and strategic relevance.Vigilance Awareness 
Initiatives
Vigilance Awareness Week 2025 was 
preceded by a three-month Special 
Campaign conducted from 18th August 
to 17th November 2025, aligned with 
the preventive vigilance framework 
of the Central Vigilance Commission. 
The campaign focused on key priority 
areas including disposal of pending 
complaints and cases, capacity building, 
asset management and digital initiatives, 
while stakeholder and customer meets strengthened transparency and 
responsiveness across the organisation. 
During the week, a series of awareness 
and engagement initiatives, including 
the Integrity Pledge, competitions, 
sensitisation programmes, seminars, walkathons, blood donation camps, 
grievance redressal camps and Gram 
Sabhas, were organised across CIL 
Headquarters, NEC, IICM Ranchi, and 
our Mumbai and Delhi desk offices. These 
initiatives helped strengthen awareness and further promote a culture of ethics 
and integrity across the organisation.

To accelerate knowledge creation and technology commercialisation, we have developed 
a strong innovation ecosystem anchored by specialised research institutions and 
academic partnerships.
The National Centre for Coal & Energy Research (NaCCER) has been established as 
the nodal institution for Coal India funded R&D activities, creating a central platform for research coordination, capability building and innovation deployment.
In addition, we now operate three dedicated Centres of Excellence focused on strategic 
innovation themes:
The newly established Centre for Sustainable Energy at IIT Madras focuses on 
sustainable materials, circular economy, mine repurposing, fleet electrification and environmental remediation.Research and innovation have long remained integral to our long term 
strategy. Our formal R&D journey began 
with the constitution of the R&D Board 
of Coal India, supported by an Apex 
Committee to guide strategic research 
priorities and ensure effective oversight. 
Both governance bodies include strong 
external expert representation, enabling 
access to specialised knowledge and 
industry best practices.
To further strengthen execution, we approved a comprehensive Policy & 
Guidelines on Research & Development 
Projects Funded by Coal India Limited 
during FY 2025-26. This policy enhances 
project governance, prioritisation and 
evaluation, ensuring greater alignment 
between research investments and 
business outcomes.
We are increasingly prioritising applied 
research with Technology Readiness 
Level (TRL) 4 and above, enabling 
faster commercial adoption and stronger 
operational impact.

Strengthening Environmental 
Stewardship Across Operations Environmental Management Framework 
Responsible environmental management 
remains integral to how we operate across 
the mining lifecycle, from mine planning 
and extraction to reclamation and closure. 
We continue to embed environmental 
considerations into operational decision 
making through structured management 
systems, pollution control measures and 
ecosystem restoration initiatives.
Our approach focuses on minimising 
environmental impact, improving resource 
efficiency and advancing progressive 
reclamation, while supporting responsible 
resource utilisation and long term 
ecological resilience.Our environmental management practices are guided by certified management 
systems, regulatory compliance and structured monitoring mechanisms that strengthen 
accountability and operational discipline.
Coal India headquarters is certified for ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015 and ISO 
50001:2018 for quality, environmental and energy management systems. ECL and MCL 
maintain integrated management system certifications covering quality, environmental 
and occupational health and safety standards. CMPDIL further strengthens governance 
through ISO certified quality systems and anti bribery management standards. 
Key Pillars of our Environmental Monitoring Landscape 
Multi Gas Detection System Ambient Air Quality Surveillance ETMS and Gas Chromatography 
Meteorological Integration 
Noise Pollution Tracking Dust Monitoring Infrastructure 
1 3 5
6
42Methanometers, Carbon Monoxide (CO) 
detectors and multi sensor monitoring 
instruments are deployed to continuously 
track atmospheric conditions across 
underground and surface operations. 
These systems enhance miner safety by 
enabling the early detection of hazardous 
gas concentrations and facilitating timely 
preventive action.A network of 164 Continuous Ambient Air 
Quality Monitoring Systems (CAAQMS) 
enables real time monitoring of key air 
quality parameters, including PM2.5, 
PM10, SOx, NOx and CO. Strategically 
installed across mine lease areas, coal 
handling facilities and surrounding communities, these systems provide 
continuous environmental surveillance. 
The monitoring data is seamlessly integrated with the Central Pollution 
Control Board (CPCB) and respective State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs), ensuring 
regulatory compliance, transparency and 
timely environmental oversight.Advanced environmental tele monitoring 
systems and gas chromatographs are deployed for detailed chemical and gaseous analyses, particularly in underground mines and operational 
workshops. These technologies facilitate 
the detection of complex air pollutants, 
support continuous environmental 
profiling, and enable timely identification 
of potential environmental and 
occupational health risks.
Meteorological parameters such as 
wind speed, wind direction, humidity, 
rainfall and temperature are monitored 
alongside air quality indicators to provide 
a comprehensive understanding of 
environmental conditions. This integrated 
approach supports predictive dust 
dispersion modelling, enables proactive 
risk assessment and facilitates the 
effective deployment of dust control and 
mitigation systems.Noise levels are monitored in decibels 
using both portable and fixed location 
monitoring devices during daytime 
and night time periods. The resulting 
data supports the implementation of 
noise control measures, helps maintain 
compliance with prescribed standards, 
and informs the development of green belts and buffer zones around sensitive receptors such as schools, hospitals and residential communities. Personal Dust Samplers (PDS) are 
deployed across critical work areas to 
monitor employee exposure to airborne 
particulates. Complementing these efforts, 
mobile dust monitoring units, stationary 
analysers and dust mapping tools are 
used to assess PM10 concentrations and 
identify areas requiring intervention. Real time particulate monitoring data supports proactive dust control 
measures, including the deployment of fog cannons, water sprinklers and other dust suppression systemsAir Quality Management

engineering controls, infrastructure upgrades and real time 
monitoring across mining and transportation corridors.Groundwater and Surface

Circular Economy and Resource RecoveryResponsible mine closure remains a 
key pillar of long term environmental 
stewardship. Mine closure planning 
integrates land restoration, ecological 
rehabilitation and post mining land use 
optimisation to support sustainable 
transition of mined landscapes.
During FY 2025-26, final closure 
approvals were received for 32 mines.

our subsidiaries have been formally 
closed in accordance with Ministry 
of Coal guidelines.Alongside strengthening environmental performance, we continue to advance cleaner 
energy and low-carbon initiatives under Mission GREEN. These interventions support 
our long term transition toward a more diversified and sustainable energy future.
We continue to explore innovative approaches to improve resource 
efficiency and unlock alternative value 
from mining by products.

IMPORTANT FINANCIAL RELATIVE RATIOS 
* Dividend per share includes Final Dividend and Interim Dividend. For FY 2025-26, final dividend of H 5.25 per share is subject to approval of shareholders in AGM.
Formulas
1 Value Added = Profit Before Tax + Finance Cost + Depreciation & Amortisation + Employee Benefit Expenses
2 Equity = Equity Share Capital + Other Equity
3 Total Debt to Equity = Borowings/Equity
4 Long Term Debt to Equity = (Long Term Borowings + Current Maturity of Long Term) / Equity
5 Current Ratio= Current Assets / Current Lilabilities
6 Return on Average Net Worth (%) = Profit After Tax (Profit for the period) / Average Net Worth
7 Capital Employed = Total Assets - Current Liabilities
8 EBIT (Earning Before Interest & Tax) = Profit Before Tax + Finance Cost 
9 Return on Average Capital Employed (%) = EBIT/Average Capital Employed
10 Debtors Turnover Ratio = Average Debtors (net of Provision) /Gross Sales *12
 For FY 25-26 & FY 24-25 Gross Sales = Sale of Products + GST on Sale of Products
11 Cost of Goods Sold = (Total Expenditure -Finance Cost - Write off - Provision-CSR-Stripping Activity Adjustment)
12 Inventory Turnover Ratio = Average Inventory of Coal /Cost of Goods Sold *12
13 EBITDA (Earning Before Interest,Tax, Depreciation & Amortisation) = Profit Before Tax + Finance Cost + 
Depreciation & Amortisation
14 EBITDA Margin (%) = EBITDA/Revenue from Operations
15 Earning Per Share = Profit After Tax (Profit for the period) attributable to owners of the company/ Weighted Average Number of Equity Shares
16 Book Value Per Share = Equity / Number of Equity Shares
17 Price Earning Ratio (P/E Ratio) = Market Price per Share /Earning Price per Share
18 Dividend Payout Ratio (%) = Dividend Per Share/Earning Per Share(H in crore) (H in crore)

Directors’ Report
Dear Stakeholders,
Financial Year (FY) 2025-26 marked a period of strategic 
transformation for Coal India Limited. While continuing to fulfil its critical role in ensuring India's energy security, the Company accelerated its transition toward becoming a diversified natural resources and energy enterprise. 
The year witnessed significant milestones including successful 
public listings of subsidiary companies, expansion into critical minerals, advancement of coal gasification projects, strengthening of renewable energy initiatives, and continued investment in evacuation infrastructure. 
Despite market headwinds and moderation in coal demand 
growth, the Company maintained robust operational performance, generated strong cash flows, and continued its track record of delivering superior shareholder returns through consistent dividend distribution. Coal India remains committed to balancing three strategic priorities: energy security, sustainable growth, and long-term value creation for stakeholders. 
1. KEY STRATEGIC ACHIEVEMENTS - STATE OF 
COMPANY’S AFFAIRS – FY 2025-26
A. Corporate and Capital Market Milestones
	 Initial Public Offer (IPO) of BCCL: Successfully 
completed the Offer for Sale (OFS) of Bharat Coking Coal Limited (BCCL) comprising 465.7 million equity shares at an issue price of H 23 per share. The issue 
was oversubscribed 146.87 times overall, leading to the successful listing of BCCL on the BSE and NSE on 19
th January 2026 with the Company retaining a 
90% subsidiary stake. 
	 Initial Public Offer (IPO) of CMPDIL: Successfully concluded the listing of Central Mine Planning & Design Institute Limited (CMPDIL) on March 30, 2026, on both the BSE and NSE. The OFS, valued at H 1,842 Crores at an issue price of H 172 per share, 
was subscribed 1.05 times, leaving the Company with a 85% subsidiary shareholding. 
	 Government Offer for Sale (OFS) in CIL: The President of India, acting through the Ministry of Coal, divested 123,279,566 equity shares (face value of H 10 each) through an OFS from May 27 
to May 29, 2026, generating a gross consideration of approximately H 5,549 Crores and bringing the 
Government of India's stake to 61.13%. 
	 Proposed IPOs and Disinvestments of MCL and SECL: 
The CIL Board accorded in-principle approval to disinvest a 25% equity stake in Mahanadi Coalfields Limited (MCL) and South Eastern Coalfields Limited (SECL) via an OFS, alongside a fresh equity issuance component of 10%. 
B. Growth and Diversification Initiatives
	 Coal Gasification Projects: Promoted plans to 
establish advanced coal gasification facilities with an estimated capital investment of approximately 
H 50,000 Crores to build a robust domestic syngas ecosystem and reduce import dependency. CIL 
initiated Expressions of Interest (EoIs) to identify technology licensors, EPC contractors, and downstream product offtakers. 
	 Critical Mineral Initiatives: Focused on national resource security by identifying critical mineral asset acquisitions overseas and executing strategic domestic exploration collaborations. 
	 Incorporation of Intermediate Holding Company (IHC) in Chile: The Board approved the setup of an IHC in Chile to actively explore and secure high-value critical mineral opportunities, including lithium, cobalt, nickel, and copper. 
	 Incorporation of Intermediate Holding Company (IHC) in Singapore: The Board authorized the establishment of an IHC in Singapore to streamline overseas asset acquisition, manage foreign investments efficiently, and provide financial flexibility for future global ventures. 
	 Rare Earth Elements (REE) Block Acquisition: Secured a vital REE exploration block at Kawalapur, Maharashtra, in January 2026, marking a significant step into the domestic critical minerals space. 
C. Renewable Energy and Clean Energy Transition
	 Coal India Limited achieved a significant milestone in its renewable energy journey with the successful commissioning of 200 MW of the 300 MW Solar Power Project at Khavda, Gujarat. The project marks a major step towards CIL’s clean energy transition strategy and reinforces its commitment to expanding its renewable energy portfolio in line with the Government of India’s energy transition and decarbonization objectives.
	 Commissioning of Solar Projects: Achieved a major green milestone by fully operationalizing the 100 MW Solar Power Plant in Banaskantha District, Gujarat, as of 31
st March 2026, receiving its formal 
commissioning certificate from the Gujarat Energy Development Agency (GEDA) on 4
th May, 2026. 
Coal India Limited has successfully commissioned 200 MW out of the 300 MW solar power capacity at Khavda, Gujarat as of 15th July, 2026. 
	 600 MW Jalaun Solar Project: Successfully won a competitive utility-scale bid to develop a 600 MW solar power project at the Jalaun Solar Park in Uttar Pradesh, reinforcing CIL's commitment to clean power deployment. 
	 Joint Venture in Rajasthan: Executed a formal Joint Venture Agreement on 10
th June, 2025, to 
incorporate CIL Rajasthan Akshay Urja Limited 
(formed 9th June, 2025) with Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut 
Utpadan Nigam Limited (RRVUNL). CIL has finalized the EPC contractor to construct 875 MW of solar power projects within the Pugal Solar Park. EPC contract to be awarded after finalization of Power Purchase Agreement (PPA).

Advanced project execution via this JV (51% CIL, 49% BHEL) incorporated on May 21, 2024, to establish a 0.66 MMTPA Coal-to-Ammonium Nitrate plant at Lakhanpur, Odisha. Environmental clearance has been obtained, and letters of award have been issued for all four Lump Sum Turnkey (LSTK) packages.

 The Company continued to focus on operational efficiency, enhanced mechanisation and productivity improvements across both opencast and underground mining operations to ensure reliable coal supplies for the country's energy requirements.

 Coal Marketing and Customer Services
 Coal India Limited continued to ensure reliable coal supplies to key consuming sectors during FY 2025-26 while strengthening marketing efficiency, enhancing customer experience and supporting the nation's energy security. The Company remained focused on meeting long-term contractual commitments, expanding market-based sales, improving coal quality management and adopting technology-driven customer service initiatives.
 Coal Offtake and Marketing Performance
 During FY 2025-26, Coal India achieved a raw coal offtake of 744.83 Million Tonnes (MT) as against 762.98 MT in 
the previous year.
 The power sector remained the Company's largest consumer, accounting for 588.01 MT of coal supplies during the year. Company-wise targets and actual offtake are provided in Annexure-5, while sector-wise dispatch details are contained in Annexure-6.
 Coal dispatch during the year was affected by certain external factors, including:	 prolonged monsoon during the second quarter;
	 temporary railway rake shortages and evacuation bottlenecks in select coalfields;
	 reduced lifting by thermal power stations due to higher pit-head coal stocks;
	 operational constraints in mine evacuation systems; and
	 localized law and order and consumer intake issues.
 Despite these challenges, the Company continued to maintain uninterrupted supplies to priority sectors through coordinated production planning and logistics management.
 Market Development and Long-Term Supply Arrangements
 Coal India continued to strengthen long-term domestic coal demand through implementation of various coal linkage schemes notified by the Government of India, including the revised SHAKTI Policy and linkage auctions for the Non-Regulated Sector (NRS).

 Diversification and New Business Initiatives
 As part of its long-term strategy to build a diversified and sustainable energy portfolio, Coal India Limited is expanding beyond its traditional coal mining business into renewable energy, coal gasification, critical minerals, thermal power generation and energy storage solutions. These initiatives are aligned with the national priorities of energy security, import substitution, resource self-reliance and the transition towards a lower-carbon economy.
 The Company's diversification roadmap is aimed at creating new growth avenues, enhancing value addition from domestic resources and ensuring long-term business sustainability while continuing to support India's growing energy requirements.
 Renewable Energy and Energy Storage
 Coa l India and its subsidiaries are actively developing 
renewable energy assets with a target of establishing 9.5 
GW of renewable energy capacity by FY 2029-30.
 During FY 2025-26, the Company strengthened its renewable energy portfolio through strategic partnerships with state utilities in Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan. A Joint Venture Agreement was executed with Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut Utpadan Nigam Limited (RRVUNL), resulting in the incorporation of CIL Rajasthan Akshay Urja Limited, which will develop 875 MW solar power projects at Pugal Solar Park, Rajasthan. Similarly, Coal India entered into a strategic partnership with U.P . Rajya Vidyut Utpadan Nigam Limited (UPRVUNL) for development of large-scale renewable energy projects in Uttar Pradesh.
 The Company also emerged as the successful bidder for a 600 MW Solar Power Project at Jalaun Solar Park, Uttar Pradesh and continued implementation of 300 MW Khavda Solar Project in Gujarat. In a major step towards creating a scalable renewable energy portfolio, Coal India entered into arrangements with Commercial and Industrial (C&I) consumers for supply of up to 4.5 GW of renewable energy through wind-solar hybrid projects. To facilitate implementation, the Company is progressing plans for development of 1.5 GW wind power capacity and 3 GW solar power capacity under the Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) framework.
 Coal India also expanded into Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), securing projects aggregating 267.5 MW / 1,070 MWh in Odisha and Telangana. As of 31
st March 
2026, the Group had installed renewable energy capacity of 357 MW, while projects aggregating approximately 523 MW were under various stages of development.
 Coal Gasification and Coal Chemicals
 Coal India is actively pursuing coal gasification as a strategic growth area to promote value addition from domestic coal resources and reduce dependence on imports of fertilizers, chemicals and natural gas.
 The Company is progressing multiple coal gasification projects through strategic joint ventures and partnerships. These include the 1.27 MMTPA Talcher Fertilizers Project, the 0.66 MMTPA Coal-to-Ammonium Nitrate Project through Bharat Coal Gasification and Chemicals Limited (BCGCL), and two Coal-to-Synthetic Natural Gas (SNG) projects being developed through Coal Gas India Limited (CGIL) and in collaboration with Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL).
 The ongoing portfolio of coal gasification projects represents investments of several thousand Crores and is expected to contribute significantly towards import substitution, development of a domestic syngas ecosystem and creation of new value chains based on indigenous coal resources.
 Building upon these initiatives, Coal India has initiated market engagement exercises for development of additional coal gasification facilities involving an estimated investment potential of approximately H 50,000 Crores.
 Critical Minerals
 Recognising the growing importance of critical minerals in clean energy technologies and advanced manufacturing, Coal India has taken strategic steps to establish a presence in this emerging sector.
 During FY 2025-26, the Company secured a Rare Earth Elements (REE) block in Maharashtra and approved the formation of overseas investment platforms in Chile and Singapore to pursue global opportunities in critical minerals. These initiatives are expected to support India's resource security objectives and strengthen Coal India's diversification portfolio.
 Thermal Power and Integrated Energy Projects
 Coal India continued to strengthen its integrated energy

16. MINES SAFETY
 Safety remains the highest priority at Coal India Limited (CIL) and is embedded in every aspect of its mining operations. Guided by its Occupational Health & Safety Policy, CIL continues to strengthen its safety culture through adoption of advanced technologies, robust risk management systems, continuous training, regulatory compliance and proactive monitoring. During FY 2025-26, several initiatives were undertaken to enhance workplace safety and reinforce the objective of achieving Zero Harm Potential (ZHP) across all mining operations.
 Occupational Health & Safety Framework
 CIL maintains a comprehensive Occupational Health & Safety (OHS) framework supported by multidisciplinary Internal Safety Organisations (ISO) across all subsidiaries.
 Key elements include:
• Comprehensive Occupational Health & Safety Policy
• Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA)-based Safety Management System
• Mine-specific Safety Management Plans (SMP)
• Principal Hazard Management Plans (PHMP)
• Trigger Action Response Plans (TARP)
• Periodic safety audits and risk assessments
• Continuous employee participation in safety management
• Dedicated Internal Safety Organisations at Corporate, Subsidiary and Area levels
 Mine safety is governed by an extensive statutory framework comprising the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, Coal Mines

 MINE EMERGENCY RESPONSE SYSTEM
 Coal India Limited (CIL) maintains a robust Mine Emergency Response System to ensure prompt and effective response to emergencies arising from mine fires, inundation, explosions, roof falls, gas incidents and other unforeseen situations. The emergency preparedness framework is supported by well-established rescue infrastructure, trained personnel, regular mock drills and statutory emergency response mechanisms across all subsidiaries.
 EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE
 CIL has established comprehensive emergency preparedness mechanisms in all mines in accordance with statutory requirements. Key initiatives include:
	 Preparation and periodic updation of Mine-specific Emergency Response and Evacuation Plans. 
	 Identification and demarcation of Emergency Escape Routes in underground mines. 
	 Conduct of regular mock drills and emergency rehearsals to assess the effectiveness of Emergency Action Plans, with participation of agencies such as the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) wherever required. 
	 Preparation of emergency checklists, communication protocols and information flow charts to facilitate coordinated and timely response during emergencies.  MINE RESCUE ORGANISATION
 CIL maintains a well-equipped and strategically located Mine Rescue Organisation to provide round-the-clock emergency response support across all mining subsidiaries.
 As on 31st March 2026, the rescue infrastructure comprised:
Rescue Infrastructure Number
Mine Rescue Stations (MRS) 6
Rescue Rooms with Refresher Training (RRRT)12
Rescue Rooms (RR) 12
 Key features of the rescue system include:
• Rescue establishments equipped with modern rescue apparatus and emergency equipment in accordance with the Mines Rescue Rules, 1985. 
• Deployment of adequately trained Rescue Trained Personnel (RTPs) and Permanent Brigade Members on a 24×7 standby basis. 
• Periodic refresher training and simulation exercises in modern rescue galleries and operational mines to maintain operational readiness. 
• Strategic location of Mine Rescue Stations and Rescue Rooms to ensure rapid mobilization during emergencies. First Aid and Emergency Response Competitions
To promote emergency preparedness and enhance first-aid capabilities, CIL regularly organizes First Aid Competitions across its subsidiaries.
During FY 2025-26, teams from all subsidiaries, including dedicated women's contingents, participated in the competition, 
demonstrating high standards of first-aid skills, emergency response preparedness and commitment to workplace safety.

 Coal India Limited (CIL) continues to strengthen its

19.  RECRUITMENT
 During the fiscal year 2025–26, Coal India Limited undertook a strategic recruitment drive to strengthen its workforce by inducting Management Trainees across Technical and Non-Technical disciplines, as well as Medical Executives through direct recruitment. This initiative not only aims to effectively address manpower requirements arising from retirements, resignations, and overall attrition, but it also ensures seamless operational continuity. Furthermore, the Company facilitated the promotion and selection of Non-Executive employees to the Executive cadre across various disciplines, thereby enhancing organizational capacity and supporting smooth hierarchical transitions within the Company. Further in alignment with CIL’s diversification strategy, the company had initiated lateral hiring for specialized and emerging roles in Renewables. This move highlights CIL’s proactive approach towards building domain expertise and enhancing organizational capability in the renewable energy sector. Inclusive Hiring Practices:
 We are committed to providing equitable employment opportunities, with a particular focus on employees from vulnerable and underrepresented groups. Our recruitment processes are designed to be transparent, inclusive, and merit-based, incorporating diverse selection panels that reflect a range of backgrounds to uphold fairness and impartiality. Special provisions are made to accommodate candidates with disabilities or specific needs, and we maintain a zero-tolerance approach towards discrimination on the grounds of caste, creed, religion, or any other personal attributes.
 Promoting Diversity and Inclusion
 Our recruitment strategy places a strong emphasis on 
fostering cultural diversity within the organization. By actively engaging Management Trainees from varied backgrounds, we cultivate a workforce enriched with diverse perspectives, skills, and experiences. This inclusive talent pool serves as a catalyst for innovation and creativity, thereby strengthening our organizational capabilities and enhancing our competitiveness in the global mining industry.
 Strategic Recruitment Initiatives
 During FY 2025-26, Coal India Limited undertook strategic recruitment initiatives to strengthen its talent pipeline by recruiting Management Trainees and Medical Executives through a transparent, merit-based and technology-enabled selection process.
 To ensure efficiency, transparency and fairness, the Company engaged a Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE) as the implementing agency for conducting the Computer-Based Test (CBT) and associated recruitment activities. The agency managed the end-to-end recruitment process, including development of the online application portal, conduct of the CBT, evaluation of candidates and timely resolution of candidate grievances, thereby ensuring a seamless and credible recruitment process.

 Coal India Limited (CIL) continues to enhance its employee welfare ecosystem through a combination of comprehensive facilities, forward-looking policies, and ongoing improvements.  HOUSING FACILITIES
 CIL and its subsidiaries provide company accommodation to all eligible employees, subject to availability and applicable regulations.  CIL offers two types of scholarships to employees’ children every year:

 POLICY
 During the FY 2025–26, Coal India Limited continued to strengthen its human resource management framework through a series of strategic policy initiatives focused 
on leadership development, employee welfare, talent acquisition, organizational mobility, and institutional strengthening. In line with the guidelines of 
the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), the Company further advanced its Succession Planning and Leadership Development Plan with emphasis on leadership pipeline creation, competency-based development, and structured talent management.
 
As part of its recruitment reforms, the Company approved the transition from GATE-based recruitment to Computer-Based Testing (CBT) for engagement of Management Trainees in all engineering disciplines, except Mining, with effect from 2025 onwards. This initiative is aimed at ensuring wider outreach and a more standardized and transparent selection process.
 During the year, amendments were also introduced in the Executive Job Rotation and Transfer Policy to enhance flexibility, transparency, and administrative efficiency in inter-subsidiary transfers. The revised provisions covered mutual transfers, spouse-ground transfers, medical-ground transfers, and temporary retention on promotion.
 Further, the Company strengthened employee welfare measures through revision of House Rent Allowance (HRA) and lease rental ceilings following the Industrial Dearness Allowance (IDA) crossing 50%. In addition, the gratuity ceiling for executives and non-unionized supervisors was enhanced from H 20 lakh to H 25 lakh with effect from 1
st October 2025.
 To reinforce employee healthcare support, full reimbursement eligibility for cancer treatment at Tata Memorial Hospital was extended to both serving and retired beneficiaries under the applicable medical schemes.
 In the area of sports promotion and employee engagement, contribution rates to the Coal India Sports Promotion Association (CISPA) Fund were revised to further strengthen sports infrastructure and activities across subsidiaries.
 Keeping in view the Company’s diversification initiatives, the Policy Cell of CIL is also undertaking measures to facilitate acquisition of specialized manpower for the Business Development Division.

 Alert Generation in SAP /ERP for Sensitive Posting: 
 As per provisions of HR Manual of CIL, all officials posted 
in sensitive position should be rotated/ transferred after completion of the stipulated tenure. Prevalent practice involves the identification and tracking of tenure completion for officials posted at sensitive positions at CIL and subsidiary companies manually. This manual process increases the likelihood of human error and makes it difficult to streamline the records. Since CIL & Subsidiary companies have already migrated to ERP , it was suggested to implement an automated alert generation system regarding sensitive posting periods through the SAP/ ERP (HR) module across CIL and its subsidiaries. For better use of IT, and to enhance transparency, System Improvement Measures (SIM) were suggested for uniform implementation across CIL and its subsidiaries which includes - Mapping of all sensitive posts of executives and non- executives in the ERP by all units/areas/subsidiaries by designated officers in line with relevant circular of CIL and any other circulars issued by CIL from time to time in respect of sensitive posting, Regular updating of records and information regarding the transfer, posting, and joining of officials in the ERP system shall be carried out, Generation of alerts for tenure completion in sensitive posts on periodic basis and placement before Competent Authority for decision.  Job rotation of officials has to be done in a periodic 
manner based on alerts generated.
 Inventory Management of Spares / Parts of P&M 
including Pumps
 Suggested for Inventory management of P&M spares/
parts, including pumps, through improved record-keeping (physical/digital) and regular auditing of procured and consumed stock. These included that the relevant details of all Plant & Machinery (P&M) items including Pumps used for de- watering in the mines, should be entered in the Asset Register duly maintained for that purpose in physical/digital form, Proper inventory management by way of record keeping of the spares procured and consumed to be ensured and Log books should be maintained at unit level for all P&M items including pumps. Details of all repairs including day to day consumption of spares/consumables should be entered in the log books with proper authentication by concerned officials. Further, Periodic audit of consumption of spares against each P&M item should be ensured at appropriate level to assess the cost of maintaining the assets vis-à-vis cost of replacement. Focused planning and review should be ensured for Asset Life Cycle Management of all P&M items.

24.  VIGILANCE DIVISION
 Coal India Ltd. operates a meticulously organized Vigilance Division located at its Corporate HQ in Kolkata, led by a Chief Vigilance Officer and supported by a diverse team of vigilance officers. Similarly, its eight subsidiaries have their independent Vigilance Units, each headed by a CVO. At the level of holding company, CVO, CIL acts as a coordinating authority between subsidiary Vigilance, CBI, Ministry of Coal and the Central Vigilance Commission. At the corporate level, CVO, CIL deals with complaints, and undertakes systemic improvements in matters affecting Coal India Limited (HQ) as well as its subsidiaries. Complaints received within the organization are addressed in alignment with CIL’s “Complaint Handling Policy” and the guidelines established by the CVC. These are processed using the Online Complaint Handling Portal from the point of receipt until resolution. As part of preventive vigilance efforts, CIL’s vigilance division conducts System Studies on various business processes with operational and financial implications, proposing specific system improvement suggestions

30. PREVENTION OF SEXUAL HARASSMENT OF 
WOMEN AT THE WORKPLACE
 Coal India Limited (CIL) has adopted a comprehensive 
Anti-Sexual Harassment Policy in accordance with the provisions of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013. Internal Committees (ICs) have been constituted at CIL Headquarters and across all subsidiary companies to address and redress complaints relating to sexual harassment.
 The Policy extends protection to all women employees, including permanent, contractual, temporary, trainee, and other eligible personnel. CIL follows a zero-tolerance approach towards sexual harassment and remains firmly committed to providing a safe, secure, dignified, and inclusive work environment that promotes mutual respect and equal opportunity for all employees.
 To facilitate effective implementation of the Policy and ensure accessibility of grievance redressal mechanisms, detailed modalities and guidelines are made available 
on the CIL website in English, Hindi, and relevant regional languages.
 As part of its continued commitment towards creating awareness and fostering a gender-sensitive workplace culture,  CIL regularly conducts awareness programmes, workshops, and training sessions on prevention of sexual harassment. During the FY 2025-26, two (02) awareness/workshop/training programmes were 
conducted for employees.

32. RISK MANAGEMENT
 Coal India Limited (CIL) has established a comprehensive Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) Framework to identify, assess, monitor and mitigate risks that could impact the achievement of its strategic and operational objectives. The Risk Management Framework was revised and approved by the Board of Directors at its 483
rd Meeting 
held on 8th October, 2025 reinforcing the Company's 
commitment to proactive risk governance and long-term value creation. Under the framework, enterprise-wide risks are systematically identified, evaluated and prioritised based on their likelihood and potential impact. Risks are classified as Risks That Matter (RTMs) and Non-RTM Major Risks, with clearly defined mitigation plans, risk owners and mitigation plan owners to ensure effective monitoring and timely implementation of risk mitigation measures.
 The  Chief Risk Officer (CRO), under the oversight of the 
Risk Management Committee of the Board, regularly reviews the risk profile of the Company and facilitates implementation of mitigation strategies across all business functions.
 Key Enterprise Risks
 As on 31st March 2026, CIL monitored six Risks That 
Matter (RTMs) and four Non-RTM Major Risks, as summarised below:
 Risks That Matter (RTMs)
	 Cyber Security Risk 
	 Business Risk arising from Captive and Commercial Coal Mining 
	 Operational Safety Risk 
	 Impact of Nationally Determined Commitments (NDCs) on Coal Demand and Production 
	 Delay in Land Acquisition and Possession for Mining Projects 
	 Delay in Obtaining Statutory Clearances 
 Non-RTM Major Risks
	 Contract Performance Risk 
	 Risk of Unviable Underground Mining Operations 
	 Technology Upgradation and Adoption 
	 Critical Manpower and Succession Planning Risk 
 Emerging and Strategic Risks
 Business Risk from Captive and Commercial Mining
 To address increasing competition from captive and commercial coal mining, CIL has undertaken several strategic initiatives, including implementation of SHAKTI 2025, enabling imported coal-based power plants to obtain domestic coal linkages, encouraging wider participation in coal auctions, including foreign bidders, and introducing customer-centric measures to enhance market competitiveness.
 Energy Transition and Climate Commitments
 Recognising the long-term implications of India's Nationally Determined Commitments (NDCs), CIL continues to diversify its business portfolio through investments in renewable energy, surface and underground coal gasification, coal bed methane (CBM), battery energy storage systems and other clean energy 
178 179
Coal India Limited
Integrated Annual Report 2025-26Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements

=== page 94 ===
initiatives, thereby strengthening business resilience and 
supporting the national energy transition.
 Cyber Security
 CIL continues to strengthen its cyber resilience through 
comprehensive IT security risk assessments, implementation of Information Security Management Systems (ISMS) across CIL and its subsidiaries, deployment of advanced endpoint security solutions, regular cyber security audits, and continuous awareness and capacity-building programmes for employees.

A.1 Note-16: Additional Notes to Standalone Financial Statements
Note 16.1.a.II. GuaranteeCoal India Limited disclosed that Performance Guarantee to BCGCL
1 was provided 
for coal to ammonium nitrate project for the purpose of availing support of H 688.50 
crores from the Ministry of Coal. The guarantee has been provided free of cost, i.e., without charging any guarantee fee from BCGCL. CIL has disclosed this fact as a contingent liability under Note-16 – Additional Notes to the Financial Statements.
Appendix A to Ind AS 109 defines a Financial Guarantee Contract as:“Contract that requires the issuer to make specified payments to reimburse the 
holder for a loss it incurs because a specified debtor fails to make payment when due in accordance with the original or modified terms of a debt instrument.
Guarantee deed specifically provides that guarantor’s (CIL) obligation constitutes 
a financial debt and CIL must indemnify the Ministry against amounts payable by BCGCL together with related costs. Therefore, CIL undertakes to compensate the Ministry, if BCGCL fails to discharge its financial obligations arising from Government funding. Thus, it is in line with the definition of a financial guarantee contract under Appendix A of Ind AS 109. Paragraph 5.1.1 of Ind AS 109 requires all financial liabilities (including financial guarantee contracts) to be recognised initially at fair value. Thus, CIL should have recognised:
1. Financial guarantee liability measured at fair value; and
2. Corresponding increase in investment in BCGCL (being a deemed capital 
contribution to its subsidiary), since the guarantee was provided without charging any fee.
However, the accounting treatment in accordance with the provisions of Ind AS 109 as financial liabilities has not been made by CIL. The fair value of the BCGCL guarantee should have been computed at inception and recognised as:
• (a) Guarantee liability in Standalone Balance Sheet; and
• (b) Additional investment in subsidiary (deemed contribution).
Further, expected credit losses, if any, should have been computed on the guarantee, 
resulting in the violation of the pr ovisions of Ind AS 109.The guarantee extended by 
Coal India Limited to BCGCL is a 
Performance Guarantee furnished to the Ministry of Coal in connection with the implementation of the Coal to Ammonium Nitrate Project for availing Government support under Category-I of the RFP . The guarantee does not secure repayment of any borrowing or other debt obtained by BCGCL.
The Performance Guarantee Deed 
has been examined with reference to the requirements of Ind AS 109. The mere presence of a compensation or reimbursement clause upon failure to fulfil the stipulated performance conditions does not, by itself, render the Deed a financial instrument or a financial guarantee contract under Appendix A of Ind AS 109. Such a clause is incidental to securing performance and does not amount to a contractual obligation in respect of a debt instrument. As the underlying arrangement is not a guarantee of any debt or borrowing of BCGCL, the Deed falls outside the scope of a financial guarantee contract under Ind AS 109. Accordingly, the requirements relating to recognition and measurement of financial guarantee contracts are not applicable.
A.2 Fair Value Measurement & Fair Value Hierarchy (Note 16(3)(b))
Paragraph 72 of Ind AS 113 requires an entity to categorise fair value measurements into three levels, wherein Level 3 includes cases having unobservable inputs for the asset or liability. Paragraphs 81–86 of Ind AS 113 state that 
Level 3  classification is appropriate 
only where significant unobservable inputs are used in determining fair value. 
Financial instruments whose fair value is based on observable market inputs, or whose carrying amount is a reasonable approximation of fair value would generally not fall within Level 3. Such instruments should ordinarily be disclosed as Level 2 since their valuation does not involve significant unobservable inputs. 
CIL classified financial assets and liabilities such as:
• Loans (H 0.72 crore), 
• Trade receivables (H 7,971.84 crore), 
• Cash and cash equivalents (H 639.06 crore), 
• Other bank balances (H 2,382.07 crore), and 
• Trade payables (H 192.31 crore) 
under Level 3, although their fair values are generally determined using observable inputs 
or are considered to approximate carrying amounts due to their short-term nature.
Consequently, the fair value hierarchy disclosure does not comply with Ind AS 113. The above resulted in incorrect disclosure of fair value hierarchy information in the Financial Statements. The matter was also not reported by the Statutory Auditors in their Audit Report.The observation pertains only to the 
presentation of the fair value hierarchy table in the additional disclosure note and does not affect the recognition, measurement, or carrying value of the Company’s financial assets. There has been no change in the financial assets disclosures during the year. Accordingly, the classification has no impact on the financial performance or financial position of the Company.
