A.1 Consolidated Balance sheet
Other current liabilities (Note-10.2) J 27,201.96 croreAbove does not include an amount of H 366.21 crore payable 
to the Mineral Area Development Authority (MADA), Urban Development Department, Government of Jharkhand.
Urban Development Department, Government of Jharkhand, 
vide notification (January 2006) imposed a levy of 1 per cent fee on the sale value of the coal and coke. As per the said notification, MADA was the authorized agency to collect the same in respect of the notified areas. The levy, so imposed, was challenged by CCL in the Jharkhand High Court. Accordingly, CCL has shown H 366.21 crore for the period of 2005-06 to 2022-23 as Contingent Liability. CCL is paying the said fee from FY 2023-24 onwards.
Hon’ble Supreme Court Judgment dated 25.07.2024 related 
to State’s power to tax mines and mineral Rights, clarified that States may levy or renew demands of tax. The demand of tax shall not operate on transactions made prior to 1 April 2005. Further, the Hon’ble Supreme court has rejected the submission regarding applicability of MADA with prospective effect.
Despite the above judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, 
CCL has shown the amount of H 366.21 crore as Contingent Liability and has not recognized the amount as liability.
As per Ind AS-37, Para 14 of Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, 
and Contingent Assets a provision shall be recognized when an entity has a present obligation (legal or constructive) as a result of a past event; it is probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits would be required to settle the obligation; and a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation.
Thus, non-recognition of the above amount as liability 
despite the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court has resulted in understatement of other current liability and expenditure and overstatement of profit for the year by  
H 366.21 crore.
This issue was commented upon in the supplementary audit 
of the Annual Accounts for the year 2024-25, but no action has been taken by the Management.The liability pertaining to the period from FY 2005–06 to FY 2022–23 has been challenged by CCL before the Hon’ble High Court of Jharkhand and the matter continues to remain sub judice.
Recognition of a provision under Ind AS 37 requires the 
existence of a present obligation arising from a past event and that an outflow of economic resources is probable. In the present case, since the matter is under active litigation and the existence of a present obligation for the past period has not been legally established, the conditions for recognizing a provision are not satisfied. Also, recognition of the liability at this stage, based solely on an interpretation of the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgment in other case, would amount to disregarding the jurisdiction of the Hon’ble High Court in this case and presuming the outcome of the pending proceedings.
Accordingly, the disclosure of the amount as a contingent 
liability is considered appropriate and has been made in compliance with Ind AS 37.
A.2 Revenue from Operation (Note 12.1): J 168400.29 crore
Revenue from operations included H 3,142.76 crore towards 
“Singrauli Punarsthapan Charge” (SPC) levied at H 300 per 
tonne with effect from 01 May 2025, pursuant to Board approval (27 February 2025). The charge was imposed by NCL on coal consumers to recover expenditure relating to the Jayant Expansion Project.
However, levy was challenged before the Hon’ble High Court 
of Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh, by power consumers citing that the charge lacked statutory backing and the burden could not be passed on to consumers. The Hon’ble High Court, granted (29 April 2025) stay on the levy. Consequently, NCL issued 
credit notes/refunds to certain consumers.Vide order dated 29.04.2025, the Hon’ble Court passed 
an interim order in a general manner on the request of the petitioner. However, the legal opinion clarified that although the order appears to be general in nature, it is to be read as applicable only to the petitioner, i.e., all members of the petitioner association, and not to others. Since the stay has been granted on the basis of the pleadings of the petitioner, NCL Management remains entitled to charge Rs. 300/- from other consumers, except the members of the petitioner association.Sl. 
No.C&AG observation Management Explanation
As per paragraph 9(e) of Indian Accounting Standard (Ind AS) 
115, revenue can be recognised only when it is probable that the entity will collect the consideration to which it expects to be entitled. Paragraph 51 of IND AS 115, state that consideration can also vary if an entity’s entitlement to the consideration is contingent on the occurrence or non-occurrence of the future event. Further, Paragraph 56 stipulates that an Entity shall include the transaction price some or all of an amount of variable consideration, only to the extent that it is highly probable that a significant reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue recognized will not occur when the uncertainty associated with the variable consideration is subsequently resolved.
Pending litigation and since reversals already initiated, recovery 
of the above amount remains uncertain. Recognition of SPC under revenue does not satisfy the collectability criterion under the provision of Ind AS 115.
The above resulted overstatement of Revenue from Operations 
and understatement of liability of H 3,142.76 crore. Profit is also 
overstated to the above extent.
The Statutory Auditor Report is also deficient to the above 
extent.Further, the Hon’ble Court, in its order dated 19.05.2025, clarified that:
“Order dated 27.02.2025 shall remain stayed till next date 
of hearing. Since entire order has been stayed, therefore respondent cannot asked petitioner to pay Singrauli Punarasthapan charges”
In view of the above, it is clear that the interim order to stay 
is applicable only to the petitioner.
Accordingly, revenue has been recognised only to the 
extent that amounts have been accepted for payment by other customers (amounting to Rs. 3,142.76 crore). Further, SPC does not fall within the definition of variable consideration under Ind AS 115.
Moreover, disclosure in this regard has already been 
provided in Note No. 12.1 of the Consolidated Financial Statements.
B.1 Additional Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements (Note-16)
Contingent LiabilitiesCIL, in respect of MCL, disclosed that “Pursuant to the 
order of Hon’ble Supreme Court in case of Mineral Area Development Authority vs SAIL upholding the levies made by State Government for usage land for mining operations, consequential financial impact if any, is presently not ascertainable. The matter of validity of ORISED act is pending at Supreme Court and been admitted for hearing. Decision on this matter is pending as on this date”.
During previous year (2024-25), legal department of Coal India 
Limited, itself estimated the liability in respect of MCL, which worked out to H 31,227.80 crore.
As per Paragraph 10 of Ind AS 37 Provisions, Contingent 
Liabilities and Contingent Assets, a possible obligation arising from past events, whose existence depends on the outcome of uncertain future events, shall be disclosed as a contingent liability.
The above note is deficient to the extent that the Company has 
not quantified the contingent liability arising out of otherwise stuck of ORISED Act.The observation regarding potential future liability arising from the rights conferred on State Governments pursuant to the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgments in MADA & Ors. v. SAIL & Ors. does not warrant disclosure of a contingent liability in the financial statements, as there exists no possible obligation— legal or constructive—arising from a past event. As noted in the observation itself, the validity of the Orissa Rural Infrastructure and Socio-Economic Development (ORISED) Act, 2004 remains under judicial consideration by a three-judge bench of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, following its quashing by the Hon’ble Orissa High Court on 05.12.2005. To date, the Government of Odisha has neither enacted a new legislation nor revived the said Act, and no demand has been raised against MCL in this regard. As per Paragraph 10 of Ind AS 37, a contingent liability exists only where there is a possible obligation arising from past events, the outcome of which depends on uncertain future events not wholly within the control of the entity, or where a present obligation exists but does not meet the recognition criteria. In the present case, neither a demand has been raised nor has any enforceable obligation arisen. Any disclosure of contingent liability based solely on the assumption that the Supreme Court may uphold the ORISED Act and The State Government may subsequently raise a demand, would be purely speculative. Such a scenario does not meet the conditions for disclosure of a contingent liability under Ind AS 37. Accordingly, the disclosure in Note 16.1.a.I.iii of consolidated financial statements is in compliance with the relevant guidance under Ind AS, Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013 and does not result in any deficiency in the presentation of the financial statements.

B.2 Other Commitments (Note 16.1.b.ii) J 5975.01 crore
Subsidiaries of CIL have not disclosed the details towards amount of H 1,73,182.89
1 crore towards contractual commitment for the 
work relating to Mine Development and Operation (MDO).
Paragraph 114 (c) (iv) (i) of Ind AS-1 on Presentation of Financial Statements states that any entity shall disclose, inter alia, other disclosure including unrecognized contractual commitments.
This has resulted in understatement of other commitment by 
H1,73,182.89 crore. Non -disclosure of the above facts resulted in deficiency in disclosure requirement of IND AS-1.The Guidance Note on Division II of Schedule III of the companies Act states
“Accordingly, the disclosures required to be made for ‘other 
commitments’ should include only those non-cancellable contractual commitments (i.e. cancellation of which will result in a penalty disproportionate to the benefits involved) based on the professional judgement of the management which are material and relevant in understanding the Financial Statements of the company and impact the decision making of the users of Financial Statements. Examples may include commitments in the nature of buy-back arrangements, commitments to fund subsidiaries and associates, non-disposal of investments in subsidiaries and undertakings, derivative related commitments, etc.”
The Mine Development and Operation (MDO) contracts 
are executory contracts for execution of coal extraction and overburden removal activities in the ordinary course of the Company’s business. Such activities have already been carried out through conventional contractual arrangements. The MDO model merely represents an alternative contractual arrangement for execution of these mining operations and does not give rise to an unconditional contractual commitment or any disproportionate penalty requiring disclosure of the aggregate estimated contract value.
Accordingly, disclosure of the aggregate estimated 
value of MDO contracts under “Commitments” is neither envisaged nor required under Ind AS 1 read with Division II of Schedule III.
Further, the disclosures in the financial statements are 
required to be made keeping in view the overarching principle under Note 4(ii) in General Instructions for Preparation of Financial Statements that “a balance shall be maintained between providing excessive detail that may not assist users of Financial Statements and not providing important information as a result of too much aggregation.
Accordingly, the CIL group believe that disclosure of the 
MDO contracts entered in the ordinary course of business under “Other Commitments” was not warranted.Sl. 
No.C&AG observation Management Explanation
B.3 Property, Plant and Equipment (Note-3.1)
Company (CCL) acquires land under the Coal Bearing Area 
(Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957 and is vested in the name of the Company. The Ministry of Coal instructed (April 2022) the coal companies to get the land records mutated in the name of the Company as an absolute owner. CCL has 16,139.75 hectares of land in its possession, out of which mutation has been done only against 677.72 hectares of land and the balance land is yet to be mutated in the name of the Company.
The above facts regarding non-mutation of land in the name 
of CCL have not been disclosed in the Notes to the financial statements. Also, the disclosure under the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order is also deficient to that extent.The disclosure of land mutation details does not fall within the reporting requirements prescribed under Ind AS or Schedule III to the Companies Act. Accordingly, no such disclosure is warranted in the financial statements.
It is also submitted that disclosures in the financial 
statements are required to be made keeping in view the overarching principle under Note 4(ii) in General Instructions for Preparation of Financial Statements that “a balance shall be maintained between providing excessive detail that may not assist users of Financial Statements and not providing important information as a result of too much aggregation.”
The status of mutation of land, required by the Administrative 
Ministry as procedural compliance, is not relevant reporting information in the financial statements.

 CIL maintains a list of identified posts for both Executives and Non-Executives for persons with benchmark disabilities.
B) Details in respect of implementation of the RPWD Act, 2016
 i. Various activities and the policy decisions 
taken for implementation of the RPWD Act, 2016 during FY 2025-26-
 A. In accordance with the provisions of The Right of 
People with Disabilities Act, 2016 and The Rights of People with Disabilities Rules, 2017, a policy named CIL Equal Opportunity Policy has been framed by CIL to ensure that all facility, technology, information and privileges are accessible to people with disabilities. 
  Salient Features of CIL Equal Opportunity policy is given below which summarizes the benefits exclusive to the Persons with disabilities: 
  1) Facility and Amenities – Physical and digital infrastructure to the accessibility standard as per requirement. 
  2) List of identified posts for both Executives and Non-Executives for persons with benchmark disabilities. 
  3) Post Recruitment and Pre promotion Training. 
  4) CIL does not deny promotion to any employee merely on the ground of disability. If an employee acquires the disability during his/her service, he/she will not be dispensed with or reduced in rank or grade. 
  5) Preference in place of posting during transfer / Promotion. 
  6) Provision for Special Casual Leave as per the provision of RPWD ACT 2016 and DPE Guidelines. 
  7) Preference in allotment of Residential Accommodation. 
  8) Providing Aids/ Assistive Devices – Assistive Devices (Including Low Vision Aids, hearing Aids with Battery), Special furniture, wheel chairs (Motorized if Required by the employee), Computer and other Hardware for use in connection with their work to improve their efficiency. 
  9) Liaison Officer to look after reservation matters relating to persons with disabilities. 
  10) Grievance redressal officer for looking after the grievances of people with disabilities.
  11) Accessibility and barrier free environment  
at work place:
   a) Ramps at entrance
   b) Railings
   c) Accessible toilets
   d) Wheel chairs
   e) Lifts/Elevators 
   f) Recruitment and selection: Relaxations/Concessions and other benefits to the Persons with Disabilities during recruitment and selection process in age/application fee/reservation in vacancies and relaxation in qualifying marks.
    Further, as per the provisions of the Right of Persons with Disabilities 2016, under Sec 34 reservation is being provided to the persons with benchmark disabilities of 1 %  each under clause (a), (b), and (c)   and   1% for persons with benchmark disabilities under clauses (d) & (e) namely:
    (i) Blindness and low vision
    (ii) Deaf and hard of hearing
    (iii) Locomotor disability including 
cerebral palsy, leprosy, cured, dwarfism, acid attack victims, and muscular dystrophy;
    (iv) Autism, intellectual disability, specific learning disability and mental illness;
    (v) Multiple disability from amongst 
persons under clauses (a) to (d) including deaf-blindness in the posts identified for each disability.

  12) Enhanced rate of Transport Subsidy to the 
Physically Handicapped (Divyang) employees under National Coal Wage agreement/ Transport allowance payable to PwD employees outside the overall ceiling of cafeteria approach under DPE guidelines.
  13) Travelling allowance (Journey fare) is paid to the attendant/escort accompanying a disabled employee during travel while on tour/training after due certification in this regard.
 B. Details of the benefits applicable to employees which includes Persons with Disabilities:
  1. Payment of Gratuity as per the statute.
  2. Coal Mines Provident Fund Scheme (CMPF): All employees of CIL/Subsidiaries are covered under the Coal Mines Provident Fund scheme with equal share of contribution from both (i.e. from the employees and the employer)
  3. Coal Mines Pension Scheme (CMPS):  All employees of CIL/Subsidiaries are covered under the Coal Mines Pension Scheme by which upon superannuation, 25% of the average emoluments are paid as monthly pension.
  4. Defined Contribution Superannuation Pension scheme (DCSPS) as part of Superannuation benefit for executives as per DPE guidelines.
  5. Facility of dependent employment and monthly monetary compensation in lieu of dependent employment as per rules.
  6. Financial assistance for laptop and mobile to executives.
  7. Financial assistance for uniform to all employees.
  8. Payment of ex-gratia in case of death in addition to the compensation under statute.
  9. Comprehensive medical facility.
  10. Comprehensive leave facility.
  11. Post retirement medical support
  12. Coverage of all employees under various welfare activities which includes persons with disabilities. ii. Allocation under various schemes for the 
benefit of persons with disabilities, the amount released and the amount utilized.

1. The Company is yet to appoint requisite number of 
Independent Directors on the Board of Directors as required under Regulation 17(1)(b) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015As per the Articles of Association of the Company, Coal India being a CPSE, the power to appoint Director vests with Govt. of India. The Company is actively pursuing with MoC for appointment of 
requisite number of Independent Directors on its Board.
2. Company has taken up the matter with Ministry of Coal, the Administrative Ministry even before vacancy arose as well as subsequent to the vacancy to arrange to appoint a Independent Director including Woman Independent Director to comply with SEBI (LoDR) regulations 2015.

Independent Director  including Woman Independent Director on its Board.

th March 2026 to 31st March 2026, the Board

Details about Technology Absorption and Research and Development (R&D) of the Company
1. R&D Setup in CIL:
 The journey of R&D in CIL started with decision of CIL 
Board in its 143rd meeting, held on 7th December 1994, 
to constitute a R&D Board headed by Chairman, CIL. Subsequently, R&D Board of CIL was strengthened by formation of an Apex Committee for R&D Board of CIL headed by Director (Technical), CIL. Both of these Committees have inclusion of 50% external members.
 The thrust area of R&D activities of CIL are (1) Mine Planning, Production, Productivity, Safety, and Exploration (2) AI/ML/IoT-based Smart Mining (3) Environment, Ecology, Conservation, and Sustainability (4) Coal Mining Waste to Wealth (5) Technology Innovation and Indigenisation (6) Alternative use of Coal (7) Renewable Energy (8) Clean Coal Technologies, Coal Beneficiation and Mineral Processing.
 In order to streamline the R&D activities in CIL, a comprehensive “Policy & Guidelines on Research & Development (R&D) Projects Funded by Coal India Limited” has been approved by CIL Board in its 388
th 
Meeting held on 12th February 2026.
 It has also been approved that National Centre for Coal & Energy Research (NaCCER) shall act as Nodal Agency for all CIL funded R&D Activities. Phase-1 of NaCCER was established at CMPDIL on 7
th October 2024. Following 
the approval of the CIL Board in its 488th meeting held 
on 12th February 2026, NaCCER has been established as 
an independent unit funded by CIL with organisational structure under the administrative control of CIL. The Board of Governors of NaCCER is constituted and headed by Chairman, CIL, which is the Apex Body of NaCCER.
 Moreover, CIL has established a new Centre of Excellence (CoE) at IIT Madras with name “Centre for Sustainable Energy (CSE)” for research in the thematic area of Sustainable Materials and Circular Economy, Mine repurposing and Fleet Electrification, Environmental Remediation and Pollution Control, Materials for Energy Transition from Coal, with at total approved outlay of H 88 Crores for the period of 5 years.
 With above mentioned CoE, CIL is now having three (03) CoEs for R&D and innovation at: (1) IIT (ISM), Dhanbad for Mining 4.0; (2) IIT Hyderabad for Clean Coal Technologies and Net Zero and (3) IIT Madras for Sustainable Energy.
 CIL’s subsidiary company have also been empowered to execute R&D projects at subsidiary level with approval of subsidiary level R&D Committee headed by CMD of the concern subsidiary.
 CIL is committed to undertake R&D projects in alignment with CIL’s core activities, business priorities and potential diversification areas. In this direction CIL has recently 
undertaken projects in the areas such as Paste Fill Mining in UG Mines, Dry-Beneficiation of Coal, Pilot Plant for Coated Spherical Purified Graphite (CSPG), Surface Hydrokinetic– Based Pumped Storage (SHK-PSP) Technology etc.
 CIL is now prioritising R&D Projects mainly through applied research. Project with Technology Readiness Level (TRL)-4 & above are being prioritized to give a momentum shift to R&D landscape of CIL.
2. Benefits derived from R&D activities in coal 
and lignite sectors
 Notable advances have been made through R&D efforts 
in coal exploration techniques
	 Introduction of mining methods like “blasting gallery and cable bolting” for recovery of coal in thick seams and shortwall mining at SECL.
	 “Controlled blasting” for removal of overburden rocks and coal in opencast mines as close as to 50m from surface structures successfully.
	 Rock Mass Rating (RMR) developed under R&D is now being used for designing support in underground mines.
	 Applying new technique using Airborne Laser Terrain Mapper and ground based Terrestrial Laser Scanner (TLS) for OB measurement.
	 To ensure the safety and to protect loss of equipment in opencast mines, Dumper Collision Avoidance System (DCAS) has been developed indigenously and was successfully undertaken at KDH opencast mine of Central Coalfields Limited (CCL).
	 Self-advancing goaf edge (mobile) chock type supports have been indigenously developed and their field trial conducted successfully at Bastacolla mine of BCCL [in coal roof] and RK-7 mine of SCCL [shale/ sand stone roof].
	 Introduction of modern technique like Ground Penetrating Radar for detection of old unapproachable water-logged workings.
	 The solar photovoltaic plant has been erected and commissioned on the roof tops of CMPDIL office buildings. The total installed capacity of the plant is 190 kW. This project reduces carbon footprint & maximizes renewable energy system.
300 301
Coal India Limited
Integrated Annual Report 2025-26Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements

=== page 155 ===
	 Under techno-economic efficacy for ANFO 
explosive, with low density, porous, thermally stabilised, Prilled Ammonium Nitrate in CIL mines, vis-à-vis other conventional explosives in terms of Powder Factor (PF), post blast analysis etc. has been established. From the above study, it was found that fragmentation using ANFO is better and cost effective in comparison to other explosives in dry condition.
	 Under project “Requirement of air in mine for Mass Production Technology’ complete ventilation studies were conducted in Continuous Miner operated mines and Long wall mines and based on analysis a norms relating to minimum air quantity framed in CM panels, as it was not practicable to provide stipulated air quantity at the Last Ventilation Connection (LVC) in mass production panels as per Regulation 153 {2(a)} of CMR-2017 as it pose problems of high dust generation and high water gauge in the main mechanical ventilator of the mine. As an outcome of this project, DGMS issued DGMS (Tech.) (S&T) Circular no. 02, Dhanbad dated 11
th April 2025 related to Guidelines on minimum 
air quantity required at Continuous miner and Long wall panels.
	 Development of guidelines for design of all tiers of shovel-dumper dump above dragline dump, with delineation of phreatic surface, within dragline dump throughout the year and validation study on two dragline mines of Coal India Limited (CIL). Based on the study, a general guideline has been developed relating to maximum height, slope of dragline and shovel dumper dump.
	 Under the project “Restoration of Orchid flora of Makum Coalfield areas of Digboi Forest Division”, fifteen hundred seedlings are multiplied and planted in re-vegetated mined out sites, nearby forest site and RFRI botanical garden with exhaustive care. Conservation and maintenance of orchid species were done at RFRI botanical garden and Tikak Colliery.
	 Bench Scale Study on reducing ash content (mineral matter) from Washery Grade Coking coal and high ash non-coking coal through oil agglomeration. Coal-Oil Agglomeration unit fabricated, installed and commissioned at NML laboratory, Jamshedpur using three types of oils i.e. sunflower oil, castor oil and pine oil for reducing the ash content of coal. Coking coal with sunflower oil shows encouraging results (Topa Coal: Ash %age reduced to 9% from 21% with 84% yield, Rajrappa Coal: Ash %age reduced to 20% from 34% with 80% yield).
	 Development of Guidelines for Increasing the Height of Overburden Dumps at Opencast Coal Mines in India. Design and developed a Large- Scale Direct Shear Testing Machine at CMPDIL for testing of representative OB dump samples from Opencast Coal mines. Steeper bench angles up to 40° and external dump height up to 120m can be considered safe based on the strength properties of OB material, in comparison to present Coal Mine Regulation 2017 which limits the individual bench angle to 37.5° and external dump heights up to 90m.
	 Capacity Building for extraction of CMM Resource within CIL Command Areas (CMPDIL & CSIRO, Australia). CMPDIL has developed a State-of-Art Laboratory facility for understanding of CBM/ CMM resources in India to assist in unconventional gas resources extraction. Project outcome will be helpful in development of CBM/CMM in CIL & other leasehold areas.
	 Under a project, the effect of blasting on opencast mine dump was investigated and prediction model of FOS for stability of the OB dump slope was recommended considering various uncertain material parameters under blast loading with different explosive densities and distances of the blasting point.
	 Under a project, a VOD measurement system was developed which can measure velocity of detonation of in-the-hole explosive as well as cartridges, booster and other accessories on the surface. The system uses fiber optic cables for high accuracy measurement. The instrument cannot be initiated without the authorisation of the user, hence authenticity of the measurement and security of the tested explosives and accessories are guaranteed. The device is developed indigenously keeping the spirit of “Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan” or “Make in India” concept.
	 The indigenously developed Ground-Based Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar system has the capability to monitor deformation from a remote location. It provides utility for generating alarms/ alerts for early warning of slope failures in mobile through SMS. This prototype system developed is being deployed and verified in an actual operational environment.
	 Under a project, indigenous development of an intrinsically safe data acquisition system (both hardware and software) was undertaken for collecting longwall pressure data and shearer position data from Jhanjra longwall panel and transfer them to a surface computer. Using this system, periodic roof weighting phenomena can be detected apart from identifying maintenance issues of shield legs such as leakage, low setting pressure, faulty sensors, etc.
	 Under a project, design and deployment of Ventilation Fan Wind Power Recovery System as an alternate source of Electrical Energy in Underground Coal Mines was undertaken in which a comprehensive analysis of generating electricity from unconventional wind sources, aiming to reduce CO
2 emissions and promote green energy, the first 
of its kind in any Indian mine.
	 A project on design of Protective Barrier Pillar against Large Water Head in Underground Coal Mines has been undertaken in which a steady-state hydro-mechanically coupled numerical modelling approach has been developed to assess the performance of PWBP (Protective Water Barrier Pillar) in underground coal mines.
	 Under a project, design and development of Drop Test Facility for Pit Bottom Buffer used in Underground Coal Mines in which a state-of-the-art drop test facility having mechanism for drop load adjustment (1 tonne – 10 tonne) and the drop height adjustment (0 – 3m) as per the requirement of the test has been developed. Test rig is equipped with load releasing mechanism (upto 10 tonne load), sensors, safety items and data acquisition system for precise and safe operation, data collection and post-processing.
	 A project was undertaken for prevention of premature failures and enhancing life of bottom rollers used in bucket wheel excavators enhance the performance and longevity of bottom rollers used in Bucket Wheel Excavators (BWEs) through material development, heat treatments, and surface engineering techniques.
	 A project was undertaken to evaluate the real-world performance of perovskite solar modules through a 45-day outdoor study. The work assessed power generation, stability under varying conditions, and long-term reliability, demonstrating consistent performance, low degradation with proper monitoring, and strong potential for practical field applications.
	 A project was undertaken for the development of an indigenous world class VR facility for demonstration and training of the mining working professionals. Nigahi Opencast Project of NCL and Jhanjra Underground Project of ECL was covered to showcase the best mining practices in VR environment. Mines Rescue Station, Dhansar was covered to showcase the best safety practices.

6. Technology Absorption:
 CIL has taken many technological initiatives in various fields across its total operational activities.
	 In underground mining, Mass Production Technology has been introduced in quite a number of mines. Continuous Miner Technology (46 nos.) have been introduced in 26 mines of CIL so far, which are under operation. Long-wall mining are in operation at Moonidih UG of BCCL and Jhanjra UG of ECL.
	 5 HWs are in operation & 4 more are at different stages of implementation of which LoA issued for 3 mines where operations are likely to be started in 2026-27.
	 Total 64 nos. of Man Riding Systems (MRS) are in operation in 46 UG mines of CIL. Out of 64 nos. of Man riding systems, 41 nos. are Chair Lift type, 9 nos. are Rail car type, 7 nos. are Free-steered vehicles, 6 nos. of Multi Utility Vehicle and 1 no. is Suspended Type Mono Rail type man riding system.	 For a few underground mines proposed with mass production technology, trackless transport system has been proposed for men and material. Accordingly, 5 Free-steered vehicles and 6 multi-utility vehicles are presently in operation in Jhanjra and Khottadih underground mines of ECL and 2 Free-steered vehicles is in operation in Churi UG mine of CCL.
	 In all the four tranches, 32 nos. of mines have been identified, out of which a total of 28 nos. of discontinued UG mine have been awarded in Revenue Sharing Mode of combined peak rated capacity of 39.28. Of these, during FY 2025-26, work was awarded of One (01) mine (Mithapur UG, ECL) endowed Peak Rated Capacity of 0.49MTY. In FY 25-26, Three (03) Revenue sharing Mines have started production (PB Project of BCCL & Gopinathpur and Chinakuri UG from ECL).
	 47 numbers of departmental Surface Miners are in operation in several opencast mines of CIL to eliminate drilling and blasting and also for facilitating selective mining.
	 GPS/ GPRS based Vehicle Tracking System [VTS] in coal transporting vehicles have been introduced to prevent theft and pilferage of coal.
	 RFID, CCTV & Boom Barrier based Weight Monitoring and Control System has been introduced. It has ensured Real Time transmission of coal weighment data to the Central Server. This has enhanced transparency in the system as well as helped reducing theft of coal during transit.
	 Fixed type Automatic sprinkler system for dust suppression in Open Cast mines-Continuous monitoring of pump drive namely Start, Stop, Trip etc. is introduced through R&D efforts.
	 CMPDIL is Principal Implementing Agency (PIA) for the development of CBM in CIL leasehold areas i.e. BCCL, ECL & SECL.
	 Jharia CBM Block-I (BCCL leasehold area) has been awarded to M/s Prabha Energy Private Limited for extraction of CBM on revenue sharing basis. The CBM Block is under Exploration Phase. In 2025-26, drilling of 3 (three) Test Wells (out of 5 planned test wells) have been completed. HF and CTU unit have been mobilized and are under commissioning at Test Well sites to take the Hydro-Fracturing Jobs.
	 For Jharia CBM Block-II, Pre-Feasibility Report prepared & approved.
	 In Jharia CBM Block (CIL-ONGC Consortium) 2 development wells completed, hydro fracturing done in 6 wells and well completion & testing done in 3 wells.
	 CMPDIL is technical consultant to CIL for the development of these blocks.	 Clean Energy Lab carried out CBM and Shale Gas specific studies under Promotional/Regional/Detailed Exploration Programme.
7. Benefits derived out of technological 
initiatives undertaken:
 Most optimum sizes of HEMMs are being provisioned 
for opencast projects which are at par with the World technology. To achieve the high production target from large opencast mines, deployment of Electric Rope (ER) shovels of 42 Cum and Dump trucks of 240 T were made during the past years, which are highest in sizes proposed in India so far. Using surface miners eliminates drilling and blasting operations in the opencast projects and as such, the problem of working very near to inhabited areas has been sorted out due to elimination of blasting vibrations. Moreover, because of possible selective mining, the chances of contamination of produced coal with extraneous materials has also been minimized.8. Details of efforts on imported technology:
 Coal India has envisaged foreign collaboration with a view to:
	 Bring in proven and advanced technologies and management skills for exploiting maximum resources from UG and OC mines, coal preparation, coal exploration and other activities.
	 An R&D pilot project for establishing Underground Coal Gasification (UCG) Technology in Indian Geo-Mining Conditions is being implemented by CMPDIL, ECL and Ergo Exergy Technology Inc. (EETI), Canada jointly. The project comprises of 02 Phases. Currently Phase-II is under progress.
	 Emphasis is also being made for diversification of R&D initiatives by taking up new projects in the field of environmental sustainability, energy management & digitization, reduction of carbon emission, renewable energy, use of AI & IoT, waste to wealth creation, deployment of new techniques in exploration etc.

FORMAT FOR THE ANNUAL REPORT ON CSR ACTIVITIES TO BE INCLUDED IN THE BOARD’S

1. Brief outline on CSR policy of the Company
 CSR policy of CIL has been framed after incorporating 
the features of the Companies Act 2013 including amendments to it and notifications issued by Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) and Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), Govt. of India from time to time. 
 Budget for CSR activities of CIL is allocated based on 2% of average net Profit of CIL (standalone) for three immediately preceding financial years OR as decided by CIL Board, subject to a maximum of H  2 per tonne of total coal 
production of immediate preceding financial year of those subsidiaries of CIL which had not incurred net loss in the immediate preceding financial year, whichever is higher. 
 CIL (HQ) undertakes CSR activities in whole of India including the areas covered by subsidiaries. CSR activities are undertaken in the themes specified in Schedule VII of Companies Act 2013. 
 CSR policy of CIL also contains broad guidelines regarding implementation, monitoring and reporting of CSR activities. The policy is governed by provisions under Companies Act, 2013 or any other act that may be introduced, Government guidelines and any other govt. instructions applicable from time to time.
 Major CSR projects undertaken in FY 2025-26 are as follows:
 1. Item – I of Schedule VII – Healthcare, Sanitation 
& Nutrition 
  a. H 21.84 cr. were utilized for the flagship project 
‘Thalassemia Bal Sewa Yojana’ (TBSY)

ANNEXURE 22
Significant and Material Orders passed by the Regulators  
or Courts etc.
Case No. 1:  C.A No. 2845 of 2017, CIL & Anr. vs. CCI & Sai 
Wardha Power Ltd and T.C. (Civil) No. 16-21 of 2023, CIL vs. CCI
a) Name of the Authority: Supreme Court
B) Brief of the Case: Allegations of abuse of dominance 
and unfair and discriminatory conduct by CIL and WCL 
by: (i) delaying FSA execution; and (ii) forcing SWPL to enter into one-sided anti-competitive Cost Plus FSAs.
 CCI held that CIL / subsidiaries were dominant in relevant market by virtue of the Coal Mines (Nationalization) Act, 1973 and the policy scheme, among other factors.
C) Corrective Action Taken:  On 5th December 2014, CIL 
filed an appeal along with an IA before the COMPAT for stay of the CCI’s direction. COMPAT heard the matter during March 2015 and October-November 2015, and vide Order dated 9
th December 2016 upheld CCI’s Order. 
CIL and WCL appealed against the COMPAT’s Order before Supreme Court.
 Given that appeals with similar issues involving CIL were pending before NCLAT, the Bench directed CIL to file a transfer petition seeking transfer of the connected matters from the NCLAT to the Supreme Court. Accordingly, a transfer petition was filed by CIL. On 22
nd March 2023, 
the Supreme Court ordered transfer of the cases before NCLAT to the Supreme Court.
 The Supreme Court vide judgment dated 15
th June 
2023, disposed of the IA for additional grounds (CIL’s argument that the Competition Act does not apply to CIL) and the Transfer Petition. The Supreme Court held that the Competition Act applies to CIL / subsidiaries but clarified that CIL will be entitled to take any defenses available under the law to demonstrate that it has not abused its dominance. The Supreme Court ordered that CIL’s appeal in the SWPL matter be decided on merits and that all connected matters from NCLAT be remitted to be decided on their own merits.
 On 11
th April 2025, WCL filed an IA before the Supreme 
Court seeking a modification to the Supreme Courts’ interim orders dated 3
rd August 2017 and 6th November 
2017, which directed CIL / WCL to supply 3,000 tonnes of coal per day (to begin with) from Ukni Deep Mine at  
H 2,100 per tonne and from Bellora Naigaon Mine at  
H 2,000 per tonne to SWPL till the matter is finally heard, as the FSA for Ukni Deep had completed its tenure. 
 Subsequently, on 6
th November 2025, WCL filed an IA 
seeking directions to SWPL to comply with its obligations under the Urdhan Mine FSA dated 3
rd April 2012 and lift the annual contracted quantity, and to pay compensation for short-lifting of coal from the Urdhan Mine under the FSA.  
Case No. 2: C.A No. 5697 of 2017, CIL v. CCI and Bijay Poddar
a) Name of the Authority: Supreme Court
b) Brief of the Case:  An information was filed alleging that 
CIL abused its dominance in relation to the terms and conditions for imposing non-reciprocal EMD under ‘Spot e-auction’ scheme making the scheme arbitrary since it imposed a penalty on bidders who failed to offer full or part of the successful bid, but not on CIL if they failed to supply coal.
 CCI passed an order against CIL stating that this amounted to CIL having abused its dominant position. CIL filed an appeal against the CCI’s order before the erstwhile COMPAT which, vide Order dated 20
th March 
2017, dismissed CIL’s appeal and directed CIL to modify terms of Spot e-auction scheme. CIL filed an Appeal before Supreme Court against the COMPAT’s said order.
 The Supreme Court vide Order dated 05
th May 2017 
granted a stay on COMPAT’s Order. Respondents filed their reply to CIL’s appeal and CIL has also filed its rejoinder.
c) Corrective Action Taken:  On 09th August 2023, the 
Respondent moved a letter to mention the matter orally before the Supreme Court as the matter had been pending for several years. Thereafter the matter has been listed for regular hearing 10
th October 2023 onwards – 
however, due to paucity of time it has not been taken up. 
Case No. 3:  Competition Appeal (AT) No. 1-3 of 2017 
(Case No. 3, 11 & 59 of 2012 before CCI) CIL & Ors. vs. CCI, Mahagenco & GSECL
a) Name of the Authority: NCLAT
b) Brief of the Case:  This case originated from 3 separate 
Information(s) filed by Mahagenco & GSECL alleging CIL and some of its subsidiaries of abuse of dominance, imposition of unfair / discriminatory conditions in FSA provisions relating to grade spillage, sampling, supply of ungraded coal, compensation for stones / oversized coal, termination, Force Majeure conditions, etc. without any bilateral discussions with TPPs. CCI vide Order dated 9
th December 2013, imposed a penalty of H 1,773 
Crores on CIL which filed an appeal before the erstwhile COMPAT. One of CIL’s contentions was that principles of natural justice had not been adhered to and the CCI members who decided the matter were not the same as those who heard the arguments. Accordingly, re-hearings took place on 17
th May 2016 before CCI which passed Order dated 24th March 2017 with similar findings as in 
the Order dated 9th December 2013. Considering the 
changes made to sampling and other clauses in FSA and the constraints imposed by various ministries upon CIL, CCI reduced the penalty to H 591 crores.
 CIL filed an appeal against CCI’s fresh order before NCLAT. Stay has been granted on operation of the Order. The opposite parties have filed replies to the appeal and rejoinders have been filed by CIL.
 Owing to pendency of the transfer petitions before Supreme Court, the proceedings were stayed. 
c) Corrective Action Taken:  Following the Supreme 
Court judgment dated 15th June 2023, the matter was 
transferred back to the NCLAT.
 CIL filed IAs 5256-5258 of 2024 on 19th July 2024, seeking 
to raise additional grounds for the NCLAT to consider the Administrative Mechanism for Resolution of disputes between central public sector enterprises (AMRCD Guidelines), for the resolution of the current dispute. 
 The matter (along with the above-mentioned IAs) was listed on 21
th August 2025, and notice was issued on the 
IAs. In the subsequent hearing on 16th September 2025, 
CCI and Mahagenco confirmed that they had filed their reply in response to IA 5256 of 2024. Counsel for CCI clarified that the reply to this IA should also be treated as a reply to IA 5257-5258 of 2024, as the contents of the IAs are identical. The NCLAT directed GSECL to file their reply to the IAs, however, GSECL has not filed its reply to the IAs. 
 CIL filed its respective rejoinders to the CCI’s reply to the IAs and Mahagenco’s reply to the IAs, on 18
th 
November 2025. 
 On 20th November 2025, the Bench clarified that the 
additional grounds raised in the IAs will be heard along with the merits of the main appeals. The Bench also permitted all parties to file short written submissions before the next hearing, if they wish to do so. 
 A written submission was filed by the CCI on 10
th January 
2026 and Mahagenco on 14th January 2026. 
Case No. 4:  Competition Appeal (AT) No. 12 of 2017, (Case 
No. 5 & 7, 37 & 44 of 2013 before CCI) & Competition Appeal (AT) No. 11 of 2017, (Case No. 8 of 2014 before CCI), CIL & Ors. vs. CCI, MPPGCL, WBPDCL & Sponge Iron Manufacturers Association & CIL & Anr. vs. CCI & GHCLa) Name of the Authority:  NCLAT
b) Brief of the Case:  This case originated from 4 separate 
Information(s) filed by MPPGCL, WBPDCL and Sponge Iron Manufacturers Association alleging CIL and all 7 subsidiaries of abuse of dominance, imposition of unfair / discriminatory conditions in FSA provisions without any bilateral discussions with TPPs to finalize the terms and conditions of FSA.
 CCI decided that CIL abused its dominant position in drafting and finalizing of FSAs, grade declaration / review, supplies through MOUs, DDQ and supply of ungraded coal. However, no penalty was imposed since it had already been imposed in Mahagenco case. CIL filed an appeal before the erstwhile COMPAT which was tagged with Mahagenco appeal. Matter was re-heard by CCI in 2016.
 In April 17, CCI passed Order re-iterating its previous findings and observations and relying heavily on Mahagenco Order. No penalty was imposed in this Order as well. CIL filed an appeal against this decision which is pending before NCLAT.
 With respect to Case No. 8 of 2014, an Information was filed by GHCL against CIL and WCL. In this case, CCI’s findings on CIL’s abuse of dominant position, were related to LOA terms and conditions, process of drafting FSA, reduction of ACQ through MOU, cumulative effect of MOU, addendum to FSA, CG extension, provisions regarding SD, sampling, grade review and DDQ clause.
 Owing to pendency of transfer petition before Supreme Court, these proceedings were stayed. 
c) Corrective Action Taken:  The Supreme Court vide 
judgment dated 15th June 2023 directed that the case be 
transferred back to NCLAT to be decided on merits. 
 CIL filed the IA No. 5311 of 2024 on 19th July 2024, seeking 
to raise additional grounds under the AMRCD Guidelines. Notice was issued on the IA on 16
th September 2025 to 
the Respondents. The CCI informed the NCLAT that the reply filed in IA 5256 of 2024 also be treated as the reply to IA 5311 of 2024. 
 WBPDCL filed its reply to the Appeal and the above-mentioned IA on 18

to serve their reply upon CIL. At the subsequent hearing on 20
th November 2025, the Bench noted the status of 
pleadings in the above-mentioned IA and directed that all remaining replies and rejoinders be filed before the

Case No. 5: Case No. 11 of 2017; KPCL vs. CIL, MCL & WCL, 
Now Competition Appeal (AT) 36 of 2018, Appeal filed by KPCL against CCI’s Order dated 16
th March 2018
a) Name of the Authority:  NCLAT 
b) Brief of the Case:  On 27th March 2017, an information 
was filed by KPCL against CIL, MCL and WCL, raising few issues which had all been dealt with by CCI in Mahagenco case.
 CCI vide Order dated 16
th March 2018, dismissed the 
complaint filed by KPCL stating that since the issues raised by KPCL had already been dealt with in previous cases. KPCL filed an appeal against CCI’s decision which is pending before NCLAT.
 Owing to pendency of transfer petition before Supreme Court, a stay on these proceedings has been ordered by the Supreme Court. NCLAT has been informed about the stay granted by Supreme Court.
 
Corrective Action Taken:  The Supreme Court vide 
judgment dated 15th June 2023 directed that the case be 
transferred back to NCLAT to be decided on merits. 
 On 5th November, 2025, KPCL filed an IA before the NCLAT, 
seeking an order from the NCLAT to link and consolidate the KPCL appeal with Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 1-3 of 2017, 11 of 2017 and 12 of 2017. On the last date of hearing (11 November 2025), KPCL sought to press the IA before the NCLAT, however, the Bench was not inclined to link and consolidate the aforementioned appeals. 
 At the subsequent hearing held on 20
th December 2025, 
counsel for KPCL submitted that an application seeking tagging of this matter with Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 1-3 of 2017, 11 of 2017 and 12 of 2017 had been filed, on the basis that the CCI findings arose from the “same order.” No such application was traceable on record, thus the Bench directed the Registry to locate it. The Bench also permitted CIL to file its reply to the IA filed by KPCL before the next date of hearing. Thereafter, CIL fled its reply to KPCL’s IA on 9
th January 2026.
 On KPCL’s consistent requests, the Bench has been directing the matter to be listed on the same date as Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 1-3 of 2017, 11 of 2017 and 12 of 2017 for administrative convenience. Pertinently, notice has not been issued thus far on the above IA filed by KPCL. 
Case No. 6:  CA. No. 2 of 2015 (TA (AT) No. 01 of 2017) 
(SWPL v. CIL & Ors)
a) Name of the Authority: NCLAT
b) Brief of the Case:  Claim of compensation filed by 
SWPL against WCL/CIL arising out of CCI and COMPAT’s Orders returning a finding of abuse of dominance against CIL on account of delay in FSA execution, faulty pricing mechanism, inferior quality of coal supplied, costs related to bank guarantees and refunds for performance incentives already paid to CIL.
 In April 15, SWPL filed an application under Section 53N of Competition Act, claiming compensation of H 908 Crores. Subsequently, on 30
th January 2017, SWPL filed 
IA with claims of over H 1,500 Crores.
 On 7th March 2017, CIL / WCL filed response to IA. NCLAT 
has not started hearing the matter as yet. CIL filed a reply to the main compensation application on 11
th September 
2017 and SWPL has filed Rejoinder. CIL has also filed additional submissions to address new issues raised by SWPL in its rejoinder.
 Since 28
th November 2017, NCLAT has been adjourning 
the matter as the main appeal against the CCI’s Order in the SWPL matter is pending before Supreme Court. On 9
th 
April 2018, SWPL filed an application seeking execution of the Order passed by COMPAT. Considering Supreme Court’s interim Order dated 10
th April 2018, NCLAT 
observed that compensation case and the execution application should await the Supreme Court’s decision.
c) Corrective Action Taken:  Pursuant to the Supreme 
Court’s interim Order dated 10th April 2018 directing 
that the compensation proceedings await the Supreme Court’s decision, the compensation proceedings haven’t been taken up. NCLAT may start hearing the compensation application in due course. Annexure 23
Corporate Governance Report 
1. Statement on Company’s Philosophy on Code 
of Governance: 
 The Board of Directors is pleased to present the Corporate 
Governance Report for the financial year ended 31st March 
2026, prepared in accordance with Regulation 34(3) and Schedule V of SEBI’s Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2015 (“Listing Regulations”).
 Corporate governance embodies our commitment to integrity, ethical conduct, transparency, and full compliance with applicable laws, rules, and guidelines. At CIL, we believe strong governance is foundational to long-term success and stakeholder trust. Our practices are designed to:
	 Promote values-driven leadership, integrity, and accountability throughout the organization
	 Ensure openness in disclosures and decision-making processes
	 Align our business conduct with both legal requirements and evolving market expectations
 CIL is dedicated to upholding these governance principles at every level, constantly striving to strengthen our board oversight, internal controls, and stakeholder engagement frameworks to meet our strategic objectives and governance benchmarks
2. Board of Directors: 
2.1 Size of the Board
	 Government Company: CIL is classified as a Government Company under Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013, with over 51% of its equity owned by the Government of India. 
	 Director Appointments:
	 Chairman Cum Managing Director: Appointed by the President of India, with terms and conditions determined by the President.
	 Other Directors: The President also appoints Whole-Time Functional Directors, Government-nominee Directors and Independent Directors
 Retirement by Rotation
 Rotational Directors:
	 Functional Directors and Government-nominee Directors are subject to retirement by rotation at the Annual General Meeting (AGM). Directors retiring under the rotation rule are eligible for reappointment in line with statutory requirements	 Exempt Directors:
	 Chairman and Independent Directors are not 
liable to retire by rotation. 
2.2 Composition of Board
 As on 31st March 2026, Board of Directors comprised of 
Chairman cum Managing Director, 5 Functional Directors, 2 Non-Executive Directors (Government Nominees) and 1 Independent Directors. CIL had requested Ministry of Coal, Govt. of India to appoint 7 more Independent directors to comply with SEBI LODR’2015.
2.3 Age limit and tenure of Directors
	 Age Limit: The Chairman & Managing Director (CMD) and other Whole-Time Functional Directors at CIL are subject to a maximum age limit of 60 years 
	 Tenure: These directors are appointed for a term 
of five years from the date of assumption of charge, or until the date of superannuation, or until further orders from the Government of India—whichever event occurs earlier. 
	 Government Nominee Directors: Directors representing the Ministry of Coal retire from the Board upon ceasing to be officials of the Ministry or until further orders from the Government of India, whichever occurs earlier.
  Independent Directors at CIL are appointed by the 
Government of India for tenure of 3 years which can be can be further extended. The directors fulfil the conditions of independence specified in: 
	 Section 149(6) of the Companies Act, 2013
	 Regulation 16(1)(b) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
	 Directorship Limits: None of the directors on CIL's Board hold directorships in more than ten public companies. 
	 Committee Membership:
	 Directors are members of not more than seven committees across all public companies in which they serve.
	 A director may serve as Chairman of not more than five committees across all public companies. 
	 Disclosure Compliance: Directors have made the necessary disclosures regarding their committee positions in other public companies as of 31
st March 2026.

(C) Scope of Audit Committee: -
 The role of the Audit Committee shall include 
the following: 
 1) oversight of the listed entity’s financial reporting process and the disclosure of its financial information to ensure that the financial statement is correct, sufficient and credible; 
 2) recommendation for appointment, remuneration and terms of appointment of auditors of the listed entity;
 3) approval of payment to statutory auditors for any other services rendered by the statutory auditors;
 4) reviewing, with the management, the annual financial statements and auditor's report thereon before submission to the board for approval, with particular reference to: 
  (a) matters required to be included in the director’s responsibility statement to be included in the board’s report in terms of clause (c) of sub-section (3) of Section 134 of the Companies Act, 2013;  
  (b) changes, if any, in accounting policies and practices and reasons for the same;   (c) major accounting entries involving estimates based on the exercise of judgment by management; 
  (d) significant adjustments made in the financial statements arising out of audit findings; 
  (e) compliance with listing and other legal requirements relating to financial statements; 
  (f) disclosure of any related party transactions; 
  (g) modified opinion(s) in the draft audit report;

(A) Brief description of terms of reference 
 Corporate Governance including Risk Assessment and 
Minimization Procedures Committee was constituted by CIL Board of Directors in its 273

held on 29th May 2014 and is in line with Regulation

rd Board Meeting held on 
29th November 2024 consisting of 1 Independent 
Director, 1 Functional Directors i.e. Director (HR) & 2 Senior Executives i.e  Chief Financial Officer & Chief Risk Officer. The Committee was further re-constituted  on 28
th March 2026 with 1 Independent 
Director, 3 Functional Directors i.e Director (HR), Director (Technical), Director (BD) and 2 Senior Executives i.e  ED (Finance) & Chief Risk Officer.
 The role of the committee shall, inter alia, include the following:
 i. To formulate a detailed risk management policy which shall include:
  (a) A framework for identification of internal and external risks specifically faced by the listed entity, in particular including financial, operational, sectoral, sustainability (particularly, ESG related risks), information, cyber security risks or any other risk as may be determined by the Committee.  (b) Measures for risk mitigation including systems and processes for internal control of identified risks.
  (c) Business continuity plan.
 ii.  To ensure that appropriate methodology, processes and systems are in place to monitor and evaluate risks associated with the business of the Company;
 iii. To monitor and oversee implementation of the risk management policy, including evaluating the adequacy of risk management systems;
 iv. To periodically review the risk management policy, at least once in two years, including by considering the changing industry dynamics and evolving complexity;
 v. To keep the board of directors informed about the nature and content of its discussions, recommendations and actions to be taken;
 vi.  
The appointment, removal and terms of remuneration of the Chief Risk Officer (if any) shall be subject to review by the Risk Management Committee.
 The Risk Management Committee shall coordinate its activities with other committees, in instances where there is any overlap with activities of such committees, as per the framework laid down by the board of directors(B) Composition, name of members and chairperson and meeting details

B) Details of Non- Compliances and Fines levied By 
BSE & NSE in last 3 years
 The Company had complied with requirements of 
Regulatory Authorities on capital markets and no penalties/strictures were imposed against it in the last three years by Stock Exchange or SEBI or any other Statutory Authority.  However, fine has been levied by BSE & NSE for the 
FY  2023-24, 2024-25 & 2025-26. This fine had 
been levied for non-compliance of some of the provisions of LO
DR with regards to appointment of required number 
of Independent Directors including a woman Independent Director, Composition of various statutory sub- committees of the Board. As on 31
st March, 2026 total penalty levied 
by both the Stock Exchanges was H 3.46 crores ( From 
20th March till 26th March). BSE Limited vide email dated 
19th April 2021, waived the fine levied for the quarters 
September 2020 and December 2020 amounting to H 0.13 
crores  and further waived H 0.13 in Jul & August’25  and 
NSE vide its email dated 10th November 2022 had waived 
the various penalties amounting to H  0.21 crores and 0.13 
crores in July & August’25  Accordingly net penalty stands at H 2.84 crores ( From 20
th March till 26th March). Out of 
which H 12.41 lakhs was paid under protest.
 Company has also informed both exchanges that being a Public Sector company, appointment of Director vests with the President of India and company took up the  matter with Ministry of Coal, its administrative Ministry 
even before the vacancy arose as well as subsequent to the vacancies with a request to appoint a woman Independent Director and requested the Stock Exchanges to waive the fine levied on the company. Company has taken up the matter with BSE & NSE to waive the fine levied for the other quarters. 
C) Details of establishment of vigil mechanism 
 Pursuant to Section 177(9) & (10) of Companies Act, 2013 and Regulation 22 of SEBI LODR Regulations 2015, the company had formulated Whistle Blower Policy to enable the individual employees to freely communicate the concerns about illegal and unethical practices in the company.  This Policy was approved in 222
nd Board 
meeting held on 12th August, 2011 and is applicable to 
CIL and its Subsidiaries. 
 CIL had provided ample opportunities to encourage directors and employees to become whistle blowers (Directors and employees who voluntarily and confidentially want to bring the unethical practices, actual or suspected fraudulent transactions in the organization to the notice of competent authority for the greater interest of the organization and the nation). It has also ensured a very robust mechanism within the framework to protect them (whistle blowers) from any kind of harm. It is hereby affirmed that no personnel have been denied access to the Audit committee.

Q) Code of Internal procedures and conduct for 
Prevention of Insider Trading.
 In pursuance to Regulation 9(1) of SEBI (Prohibition of 
Insider Trading) Regulations 2015, CIL had adopted Code of Internal Procedures and Conduct for Prevention of Insider Trading in Securities of Coal India Limited with the objective of preventing purchase and/or sale of shares of Company by an insider on the basis of unpublished price sensitive information.  e. Health and Safety Initiatives for Human Resources:  
  Safety is a core value and strategic priority of Coal India Limited (CIL). To ensure a safe and healthy work environment, CIL has implemented a comprehensive Occupational Health & Safety Policy across all mines and establishments. Internal Safety Organizations (ISO) in all subsidiaries support compliance with statutory safety requirements and promote a strong safety culture. 
  Ministry of Coal assigned ‘Development of Al Analytics for Mine Safety Inspection Reports by – ‘ISO’, ‘Safety Committee’ and DGMS enabling proactive identification of issues and rectification thereof - All subsidiaries’ as target/milestone for CIL under the compliance parameter ‘Steps and initiative taken for Health and Safety improvement of Human Resources in CPSEs’ of MoU for FY 2025-26 and communicated to CIL on 17
th July 2025.
  Accordingly, a Safety AI Analytics Dashboard has been developed in-house at CIL to transform free-text mine inspection violation reports into structured, actionable insights using a fine-tuned AI model. The model automatically classifies violations by category, required action, and responsibility level (Mine, Area, or HQ), reducing manual effort and errors. The dashboard enables proactive safety monitoring and quick identification of recurring or high-risk issues for better governance.
  The key initiatives undertaken by CIL to promote a healthy and safe work environment include: 
i. Internal Safety Organization (ISO): Multi-
disciplinary teams assist management in implementing safety policies and ensuring compliance with mining regulations.
ii. Safety Management Plans (SMPs): Mine-specific risk assessments are conducted, and appropriate control measures are implemented to mitigate identified hazards.
iii. Principal Hazards Management Plans (PHMPs): Plans are developed to identify and manage major hazards and prevent disaster scenarios. 
iv. Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs): Risk-based SOPs are established to ensure safe and standardized mining operations. 
v. Safety Audits and Inspections: Regular audits and inspections by multidisciplinary teams and statutory officials help identify gaps and improve safety performance.
vi. Technology Adoption: Modern technologies such as Mass Production Technology, Surface Miners, Highwall Mining, mechanized roof bolting, man-riding systems, and advanced HEMM are deployed to enhance safety and productivity. 
vii. Strata and Ground Control: Scientific strata management practices, including Strata Control and Monitoring Plan (SCAMP) and monitoring instruments, are used to maintain mine stability. 
viii. Mine Environment Monitoring: Advanced instruments such as gas detectors, methanometers, CO detectors, and Environmental Tele-Monitoring Systems ensure continuous monitoring of mine conditions. 
ix. Water Danger Management: Comprehensive plans, adequate pumping arrangements, embankments, and regular surveys are implemented to prevent water-related hazards. 
x. Open Cast Mine Safety Measures: Mine-specific traffic management systems, proximity warning devices, fire detection systems, GPS-based truck dispatch systems, separate Light Motor Vehicle (LMV) roads, and high-mast flags improve operational safety. 
xi. Training and Skill Development: Employees receive initial, refresher, on-the-job, and

simulator-based safety training to enhance 
competency and awareness.
xii. Emergency Preparedness: Emergency Response and Evacuation Plans (EREP) are implemented, supported by regular mock drills. 
xiii. Safety Awareness Programs: Safety campaigns, talks, oaths, posters, and other awareness initiatives strengthen safety consciousness among employees. 
xiv. Centralized Safety Monitoring: The CIL Safety Information System (CSIS) provides online monitoring of key safety parameters, supporting continuous improvement and regulatory compliance.
  Through these initiatives, CIL remains committed to achieving its goal of Zero Harm Potential (ZHP) and ensuring safe, sustainable mining operations.

1.0 INDUSTRY STRUCTURE AND DEVELOPMENT 
 Coal continues to be India’s most significant indigenous 
energy resource, serving as a cornerstone of the nation’s energy security and a driving force behind its economic growth and industrial development. With its abundant availability, cost-effectiveness, and reliability, coal remains a strategic asset in sustaining India’s power generation and supporting the nation’s transition toward energy self-reliance.
 As on 31
st March 2026, India's coal-based power 
generation capacity stands at ~229 GW out of a total installed capacity of ~533 GW i.e. ~42 % share of total installed capacity, underscoring coal's continued indispensable role in providing reliable baseload power and maintaining stable energy basket, affordable, and uninterrupted electricity supply nationwide.
 India has emerged as the second-largest producer of coal globally, with a production of 1,040.83 Million Tonnes (MT) during the FY 2025-26. The sector remains largely dominated by public sector enterprises, primarily Coal India Limited (CIL) and Singareni Collieries Company Limited (SCCL), which continue to be the bedrock of domestic coal production.Management Discussion and Analysis Report 
 Coal India Limited, with its seven wholly owned coal producing subsidiaries and one mine planning and consultancy arm, maintained its position as the largest coal-producing company in the world, registering a production of 768.19 MT during FY 2025-26. This accounts for nearly 74% of India’s total coal output, reinforcing CIL’s strategic importance. CIL continues to meet about 40% of the country’s primary commercial energy requirement, underscoring its strategic importance in India’s energy landscape.
 Looking ahead, coal is poised to remain a dominant fuel in India’s energy portfolio. As envisioned in the Vision @2047 roadmap, coal will continue to be a pivotal component in securing the country’s energy future. While the growth in coal demand may moderate post-2035, absolute demand is expected to remain steady or increase, driven by sustained base load requirements.
 From a resource availability perspective, coal remains the most abundant fossil fuel in India. According to the Geological Survey of India, the total geological resources of coal in the country are estimated at ~401 Billion Tonnes as on 1st April 2025, providing a robust foundation for long-term planning and energy security.
 The highlights of inventory of Geological Resources of Indian Coal (as on 01.04.2025), prepared by the Geological Survey of India is tabulated below:
	 A total of 401 BT of geological resources of coal have so far been estimated in India, up to the maximum depth of 1200 m. Out of the total resources, the Gondwana coalfields account for 399 BT (99.5%), while the Tertiary coalfields of Himalayan region contribute 2 BT (0.5%) of coal resources. 4.0 OUTLOOK:
 CIL has envisaged coal supply target of 850.24 MT in FY 2026-27 which is a growth of more than 14% over the previous year’s achievement. About 79% of the total despatch would be consumed by power sector only.
 With future domestic demand in mind, CIL has revised its coal production programme and a strategic coal production roadmap i.e. ~1BT by FY 2029-30. This plan entails optimising production across all CIL subsidiaries and delineating various enabling activities necessary to realise this ambitious target. These activities encompass securing statutory clearances, land acquisition and possession, ensuring rehabilitation and resettlement (R&R), procuring equipment, and enhancing evacuation infrastructure such as rail lines and coal handling plants.
 For sustainability and growth, thrust on minimising the environmental impact is laid for qualitative improvement in coal production through selective mining, beneficiation & blending, enhancing production from U/G mines and diversifying into clean coal technologies.
 CIL has planned a capital investment of H 16,500 Crores for maintaining its volume growth in FY 2026-27 and beyond. In addition, the company has also envisaged for investing substantial amount in different schemes in FY 2026-27 such as development of railway infrastructure project, solar power, Thermal Power Plants, Coal Bed Methane (CBM), revival of fertiliser plants etc
 Marketing Outlook: 
 The total power generation (incl. RES) in the country grew to about 1844.5 BU clocking a growth of 0.9 %. 
The coal-based generation in the country for FY 2025-26  
was 1250 BU with a (-)3.7 % growth over the previous year. The domestic coal based generation was 1174.4 BU {(-)2.3% growth over previous year}. Considering the growth of power generation and consequential increase in demand, the offtake target of FY 2025-26 was 900.24 MT. The demand from power sector was 668 MT against which Coal India Limited (CIL) supplied 588.01 MT, achieving 88% materialisation.
 The coal supply to Non Regulated Sector(NRS) was 155.5 MT (7.0 % growth over previous year) which is the highest supply to NRS in any given year.
 The e-auction coal booking during FY 2025-26 was 101.72 MT against 89.38 MT during previous year. The premium on e-auction during FY 2025-26 was 46 % as against 48 % in previous FY.
 Fuel Supply Agreement (FSA) commitment for Power Sector, Non-Power and bridge linkage were at about 793.90 Million Tonne Per Annum (MTPA) as on 31.03.2026. The demand of CIL coal from Power sector as per Ministry of Coal for FY 2026-27 is 669.80 MT. The yearly target for FY 2026-27 has been set at about 850.24 MT so as to cater to the entire demand of power sector, NRS and also to substitute the substitutable imported coal in the country. In order to tap the potential future market for coal consumption and explore alternative uses of domestic coal, CIL intends to offer more coking coal to steel sector and also supply coal for upcoming coal gasification projects. 
 Mechanised and Computerised Loading
 Coal India Limited (CIL) had an installed rapid loading capacity of 151 MTPA as of August 2019. In addition to this, CIL has undertaken significant initiatives to enhance mechanised coal transportation and loading systems under its First Mile Connectivity (FMC) projects. A total of 72 FMC projects have been planned to be implemented in four phases, with an aggregate capacity of 843 MTY. As of FY 2025–26, FMC projects with a cumulative capacity of 432 MTY have been operationalised. Upon completion of all FMC projects, CIL’s total mechanised/rapid loading capacity is projected to reach 994 MTY by FY 2028–29.
 The share of SILO loading is expected to grow upto 39% in the FY 2026-27.
 In order to understand the requirements of the consumers, CIL is conducting quarterly zone-wise consumer meeting with both power and non-power consumers separately. Further, subsidiaries also conduct meeting with the consumers at regular intervals. In addition, to promote ease of doing business, CIL has set up a Consumer Grievance Redressal Mechanism to redress the grievances of consumers related to coal supplies and other related issues. 
 Customer satisfaction through quality assurance and transparency in business operations have been priority areas for CIL. The initiatives taken to build Consumers’ confidence and satisfaction include supply of sized coal as per FSA provisions, extension of third-party sampling facility to all sectors of consumers under all schemes through deployment of empanelled Third-Party Agencies (TPA) as per the choice of consumer, Collection of samples through Auto Mechanical Samplers at Silo Loading points, Operationalisation Mechanical Augurs for coal sample collection, providing live camera feed to the customers for observing sample collection and preparation process, timely issuance of credit/ debit notes on quality grounds etc.  At present, twelve independent Third Party sampling agencies have been empanelled. Out of these, 10 agencies have been empanelled by Power Finance Corporation Ltd (PFCL) under Ministry of Power and 2 by CIL to cater to both power and non-power sector, giving consumers a wide option to choose from the empanelled agencies. As a result of conscious and continuous measures taken towards quality maintenance, a) The gap between the weighted average of declared and analysed GCV of coal based on results received for FY 2025-26 is only 56.7 Kcal/kg which is well within the GCV band of same Grade and b) The final grade conformity including referee for FY 2025-26 is 86%. 
 Coal India Limited has significantly advanced transparency and efficiency in its operations through the Online Reconciliation Portal, which integrates quantity, quality, and finance data into a unified digital framework. Widely adopted by power sector utilities, captive power plants, CPSEs, and non-regulated sector consumers, the portal has facilitated over 1,600 joint reconciliation statements, thereby reducing disputes and strengthening consumer confidence. By offering a comprehensive suite of services—including customer profiles, contracts, payment tracking, railway receipt details, and invoice records in downloadable formats—the platform has streamlined settlements and provided a one-stop solution for stakeholders. This digital transformation has enhanced ease of doing business and reinforced CIL’s commitment to accountability and operational excellence.

 Outlook for Sustainable Growth:
 1. Introduction
  Coal India Limited (CIL), as the largest coal mining company and a key national energy asset, has been taking extensive steps to diversify into renewable energy in alignment with India's clean energy transition. CIL's initiatives support the national target of achieving 500 GW of non-fossil fuel-based capacity by 2030 and contribute substantially to reducing the carbon footprint of government-owned industrial infrastructure. This note summarises the status, progress, and direction of CIL's renewable energy initiatives.
 2. PM Surya Ghar Yojna - Rooftop Solar Implementation across CIL
  Coal India Limited (CIL) has successfully achieved complete saturation of rooftop solar installations across eligible administrative, residential, and operational buildings of CIL and its subsidiaries under the PM Surya Ghar Yojana. A total rooftop solar capacity of 35.19 MW has been installed. The achievement reflects CIL's proactive contribution towards promotion of renewable energy and advancement of the Government of India's sustainability and energy transition goals.
 3. Solar Energy Expansion - Ground-Mounted and Utility-Scale Projects
  Solar power deployment forms the core of CIL's renewable energy diversification strategy. CIL aims to develop significant solar capacity through multiple implementation routes. The company has committed to achieving 3,000 MW of solar capacity by FY 2027-28 as part of its internal net-zero target. This planned capacity addition will subsequently scale-up to 9,500 MW by FY 2029-30.
  To meet these targets, CIL is adopting a blended development strategy that includes joint ventures with state generating companies, tariff-based competitive bidding for sale of power through PPA, captive projects on own land for internal consumption, and projects developed for commercial and industrial (C&I) consumers. Till date CIL has an installed capacity of 357.65 MW and projects of around 523.50 MW are under execution and expected to be completed by FY 26-27.
  
Major partnerships with Rajasthan Vidyut Utpadan Nigam Limited (RVUNL) and Uttar Pradesh Rajya Vidyut Utpadan Nigam Limited (UPRVUNL) are central to CIL's multi- gigawatt solar rollout. Concurrently, CIL also developing solar capacity at Khavda, Gujarat and multiple subsidiary locations.
 4. Major Ongoing Renewable Energy Projects of CIL
  In Gujarat, CIL is progressing with a 300 MW solar project in the Khavda renewable energy park. Across subsidiaries, a robust pipeline of ground-mounted and rooftop projects is being implemented, including 223.50 MW currently under construction and around 344.25 MW under DPR or feasibility assessment. These projects span BCCL, CCL, ECL, MCL, NCL, SECL, and WCL, demonstrating sustained investment across coalfields.
  CIL is also exploring hybrid solar-wind-BESS to expand its capacity pipeline. Already CIL has signed BESPA for 187.5 MW/750 MWh (TGGENCO) and for 80 MW/320 MWh (GRIDCO). Also, CIL has won TBCB tender of NHPC for MW Solar Project at Jalaun Solar Park, UP .
 5. Wind Energy Programme
  CIL has initiated looping wind energy portfolio in wind-rich regions i.e. Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Andhra Pradesh.
 6. Governance, Monitoring, and Institutional Mechanisms
  CIL has established a dedicated Renewable Energy Division at its headquarters to steer its transition toward clean energy. CMPDIL, as the project management consultant, supports site development, DPR preparation, and technical vetting across subsidiaries. 
7. Year-Wise Renewable Capacity Targets (Progressive)
  CIL has formulated a structured capacity addition pathway extending to FY 2029-30. The progressive year-wise renewable capacity (installed and planned) is as follows:
